passages.title: Oath by the clear Arabic Book
passages.tafsir:
Surah az-Zukhruf opens with two disconnected letters, an oath sworn by the Qur'an itself, and then two statements about that same Qur'an: what it is down here among us — an Arabic recitation, made so that people would actually use their minds on it — and what it is up there with Allah, in the Mother of the Book, exalted and full of wisdom. What holds ayat 1–4 together is a single subject seen from two directions: the Book in your hands, and the Book in the presence of your Lord.

## Where the surah stands

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that this surah is Makki, adding that Muqatil (may Allah have mercy on him) said that ayah 45 is Madani, and that according to another view, reported from Ruh ul-Maʿani, the surah was revealed in Heaven during Laylat al-Miʿraj — and it closes the matter with "Allah knows best." That last phrase is worth noticing: where the transmitted reports genuinely differ, the commentary lays them side by side rather than forcing one.

## Ayah 1: Ḥā-Mīm

Two letters, recited as letters. On these, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly: "Ha Meem — only Allah knows its meaning." That restraint is itself an answer. A believer loses nothing by meeting a place in the Qur'an where the honest response is to hand the meaning back to the One who spoke it. Notice too what the letters do to a listener: the surah begins with something you cannot decode — and then, in the very next breath, calls this Book *clear*.

## Ayah 2: an oath sworn by the Book

**Why Allah swears at all.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the working principle: the Book sworn by in this ayah is the Holy Qur'an, and whenever Allah swears by anything, the oath is usually an argument for the statement that follows. The thing sworn by is not a random witness; it is evidence. So swearing here by the Qur'an is an indication that the Qur'an — by virtue of being a miracle — is a proof in itself of its being a Divine Book. Nothing external is produced; the text stands up and testifies for itself.

**"Al-Kitab al-Mubin" — the clear Book.** Ibn Kathir explains *mubin* as "plain and clear in both wording and meaning, because it was revealed in the language of the Arabs, which is the most eloquent language for communication among people." Two layers, then: the wording is clear, and what the wording conveys is clear. And the reason he gives for that clarity is not mystical but linguistic — the Book came in the most eloquent language people have for communicating with one another.

**But clear in what sense?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precision that saves the reader from a common mistake. To call it a "manifest Book" means that its subjects — consisting of exhortations and advice — are easily understandable. It does *not* mean that deducing the precepts of the Shariʿah from it is easy; that, it says, is certainly a difficult job which cannot be performed without the complete capability of *ijtihad* — the trained, disciplined effort of a qualified scholar to derive legal rulings from the sources. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān anchors this on Allah's words, "And indeed We have made the Qur'an easy for seeking advice. So, is there one to seek advice?" (54:17): what is declared easy there is *taking advice*, not legislating. It does not necessarily follow from that ayah that ijtihad and inferring injunctions are easy too; rather, it is proved through other evidences that full expertise in the related subjects is a necessary condition for that exercise.

This is a balance worth carrying. Open the Qur'an expecting to be moved, warned, consoled and corrected — that is what it was made clear for. Do not open it expecting to manufacture rulings — that is a specialist's labour, and the Book's own clarity is not a licence for it.

## Ayah 3: "an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand"

Ibn Kathir works through this ayah phrase by phrase. "Verily, We have made it" — *jaʿalnahu* — he glosses as "revealed it." "A Qur'an in Arabic" means in the language of the Arabs, eloquent and clear. And "that you may be able to understand" means that you may understand it and ponder its meanings. He points to the parallel in 26:195, that it came down "in the plain Arabic language."

One thing is worth pausing on: the purpose clause. The Book was not sent in Arabic merely so that it could be recited beautifully. Ayah 3 states a *purpose*: so that you might comprehend. And Ibn Kathir's gloss adds the second half that we tend to drop — not only "understand it" but "ponder its meanings." Recitation that never becomes reflection has stopped short of the reason the Book was put into a language human beings can follow.

For those of us who do not have Arabic natively, the ayah still lands. The Book was placed inside human speech so that it could be understood and its meanings pondered. Every hour spent getting closer to that language — or to a careful translation and a sound commentary — is work directly along the grain of what ayah 3 says Allah intended.

## Ayah 4: and with Allah, it is in the Mother of the Book

Ayah 3 looked down at the Book among people. Ayah 4 lifts the eyes: "And verily, it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, indeed exalted, full of wisdom."

Ibn Kathir states the purpose of the ayah before its words: this "explains the high status of the Qur'an among the hosts on high" — that is, among the angels — "so that the people of earth will respect it, venerate it and obey it." The information is given in order to produce an attitude. You are told how this Book is regarded in the highest assembly precisely so that your own handling of it will match.

Then the phrases:

- **"And verily, it"** — Ibn Kathir: this refers to the Qur'an.
- **"is in the Mother of the Book" (fi Umm al-Kitab)** — meaning al-Lawh al-Mahfuz, the Preserved Tablet. Ibn Kathir reports this as the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. *Umm* means "mother," and here it carries the sense of source and origin.
- **"with Us" (ladayna)** — meaning, in Our presence. Ibn Kathir reports this as the view of Qatadah and others.
- **"indeed exalted" (la-ʿaliyyun)** — meaning that it occupies a position of honour and virtue. This too Ibn Kathir reports from Qatadah.
- **"full of wisdom" (ḥakim)** — Ibn Kathir: meaning clear, with no confusion or deviation.

Set that last gloss beside ayah 2. *Mubin* said the Book is plain and clear in wording and meaning; *ḥakim*, as Ibn Kathir reads it, says it is clear with nothing confused in it and nothing deviating. Its clarity down here is not a simplification made for our benefit; it reflects what the Book is where it is kept.

Ibn Kathir then gathers other ayat that say the same thing about the Qur'an's standing: "That is indeed an honourable recitation, in a Book well-guarded, which none can touch but the pure — a revelation from the Lord of all that exists" (56:77–80); and "Nay, indeed it is an admonition. So whoever wills, let him pay attention to it. It is in Records held in honour, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes — honourable and obedient" (80:11–16). All of this, he says, indicates its noble status and virtue.

## Holding ayat 1–4 together

Read as one unit, the movement is deliberate:

1. **Ḥā-Mīm** — letters whose meaning only Allah knows (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān), so the surah begins by placing you before something greater than your comprehension.
2. **By the clear Book** — Allah swears by it, and the oath *is* the argument: the Qur'an, being a miracle, is a proof in itself that it is a Divine Book (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān), plain and clear in wording and in meaning (Ibn Kathir).
3. **An Arabic Qur'an, that you may understand** — that clarity took on the most eloquent language people have, so that minds would understand it and ponder its meanings.
4. **In the Mother of the Book, exalted, full of wisdom** — and lest anyone mistake accessibility for ordinariness, the same Book is in the Preserved Tablet, in Allah's presence, high in status among the hosts on high.

The two halves answer opposite temptations. Because the Book is in human language, you may start treating it casually — ayah 4 corrects that. Because the Book is exalted in the Preserved Tablet, you may decide it is beyond you — ayah 3 corrects that. It is near enough to be understood and high enough to be revered, and the believer is asked to hold both at once.

## What it asks of us

Ibn Kathir supplies the practical conclusion himself, and it is a short, testable list: that the people of earth **respect** this Qur'an, **venerate** it, and **obey** it. Respect in how we handle and approach it. Veneration in the attention we bring to it, knowing now where it comes from. Obedience in exactly the part Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls easily understandable — the exhortations and advice — while leaving the deduction of Shariʿah rulings to those with the full capability of ijtihad.

And ayah 3 sets the standard for how we read: not recitation alone, but understanding and pondering the meanings. That is the stated reason it was put into human speech at all.

passages.title: Every prophet mocked, every mightier people destroyed
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat answer a question that hangs in the air after the opening of the sūrah. Allah has just sworn by the manifest Book, said that He made it a Qur'an in Arabic so that people may understand it and ponder its meanings, and said that with Him, in the Mother of the Book, it is exalted and full of wisdom. So a listener might ask: if that is what this Book is, and the Prophet's own people are rejecting it — why does the revelation keep coming? Ayah 5 puts that very question in Allah's own voice. Ayat 6–8 then widen the frame from Quraysh to the communities of old: no prophet came to a people without being mocked, and the mockers did not escape the consequence.

## Ayah 5: the question that is really an answer

**"Shall We then take away the Reminder from you, because you are a people excessive?"**

*Al-dhikr* — "the Reminder" — is the Qur'an itself; Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase directly as "the Reminder (this Qur'an)". It is a name that tells you what revelation is *for*. Among the ayat Ibn Kathir brings to show the Qur'an's honoured status is one that names it in the same register: *"Nay, indeed it is an admonition. So whoever wills, let him pay attention to it"* (80:11–12).

*Musrifīn* is rendered "excessive" here, and "transgressing" in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — a people who have gone past the limits set for them. The description is not softened. Allah is describing people who had run past the line, and asking them what they imagine should follow.

The ayah is put as a question rather than a statement, and the answer is left for the listener to draw himself. The commentators give two ways of drawing it, and Ibn Kathir preserves both side by side.

**First reading: "Do you think you will simply be let off?"** Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Abu Salih, Mujahid and As-Suddi all understood the ayah to mean: *do you think that We will forgive you and not punish you, when you do not do as you have been commanded?* This is the reading Ibn Jarir favoured, and the one Ibn Kathir places first. On this understanding, the ayah is a warning shaped as a question. Being addressed by revelation is not a licence. To have the Reminder recited to you and to keep transgressing anyway is not a reason for Allah to overlook the matter.

**Second reading: "Should We withdraw the Reminder from you because of what you are?"** Ibn Kathir then quotes Qatadah, and the words are worth sitting with: *"By Allah, if this Qur'an had been taken away when the first generations of this Ummah rejected it, they would have been doomed, but Allah by His mercy persisted in sending it and calling them to it for twenty years, or for as long as He willed."*

Ibn Kathir calls what Qatadah said "very good", and explains his point: Allah, by His grace and mercy towards His creation, did not stop calling them to the truth and to the wise Reminder — that is, the Qur'an — even though they were heedless and turned away from it. He sent it so that those who were decreed to be guided might be guided by it, and so that proof might be established against the others.

Notice what that does to the ayah. The very people described as *musrifīn* were still being recited to. The Reminder was not switched off the moment it was rejected — and on Qatadah's reckoning, that persistence is the reason the first generations of this Ummah were not doomed.

The two readings are not in conflict. The first says: rejection has a consequence. The second says: the calling continued anyway, by a mercy the hearers did nothing to deserve. Together they leave the listener with no room either for complacency or for despair.

## What Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out: never write anyone off

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes the second sense and pulls a practical lesson out of it, under the heading *"A Preacher must not give up his preaching due to disappointment."* Its reading of the ayah: *We will not give up advising you through the Qur'an, no matter how rebellious and disobedient you may become.*

And then the application, in its own words: the person who is engaged in preaching and inviting others towards Islam should carry the message to everybody; he must not give up preaching to some people or any group simply because they are non-believers, highly irreligious, sinners and transgressors.

This is a demanding standard, and it comes with the highest possible warrant: Allah did not withdraw the Reminder from people He had just called *musrifīn*. If the caller is tempted to conclude that a certain person is beyond reach, that a certain family member has heard it too many times, that a certain crowd is too far gone — the ayah has already answered him. Ibn Kathir's own explanation adds a second reason the conveying is not wasted even where guidance does not take root: proof is thereby established.

## Ayat 6–7: a consolation, not just a history lesson

Ibn Kathir marks the turn at ayah 6 explicitly, under the heading *"Consolation to the Prophet ﷺ for the Disbelief of Quraysh"*: *"Then Allah consoles His Prophet ﷺ for the disbelief of his people, and commands him to bear it with patience."* That heading is the key to reading these two ayat. They are not a neutral survey of religious history. They are Allah speaking to a man whose own people were rejecting and mocking him, telling him what he is standing in the middle of.

**"And how many a Prophet have We sent amongst the men of old"** (ayah 6). Ibn Kathir explains "the men of old" as meaning among the sects — the communities — of old. Prophethood was not a one-off event in Makkah; prophets were sent to community after community before.

**"And never came there a Prophet to them but they used to mock at him"** (ayah 7). Ibn Kathir's gloss is brief and exact: *they disbelieved him and mocked at him.* The ayah states this of prophets as such, across those communities of old — not of some unlucky few.

So when Quraysh mocked the Prophet ﷺ, nothing unprecedented was happening. Mockery had met the messengers before him; it is not evidence against the one who is mocked. That is the consolation. And it is why the command Ibn Kathir names alongside it is *patience* — Allah consoles His Prophet ﷺ for the disbelief of his people and commands him to bear it with patience.

## Ayah 8: the pattern completed

**"Then We destroyed men stronger in power than these, and the example of the ancients has passed away."**

Ibn Kathir spells out the address: *'We destroyed those who disbelieved in the Messengers, and they were stronger in power than these who disbelieve in you, O Muhammad.'*

The comparison is aimed straight at Quraysh. They are told that on the scale of power they are not even the strongest case: those destroyed for disbelieving in the Messengers sent to them were mightier than these.

Ibn Kathir connects this to a call the Qur'an makes elsewhere, citing it as a parallel: *"Have they not traveled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them? They were more in number than them and mightier in strength"* (40:82) — and he notes that there are many similar ayat. The invitation in that cross-reference is to go and look at how those before ended.

**"And the example of the ancients has passed away."** On this closing phrase, Ibn Kathir preserves three explanations rather than choosing one:

- **Mujahid**: "The way of their life."
- **Qatadah**: "Their punishment."
- **Others**: "Their lesson" — that is, *'We made them a lesson for those disbelievers who came after them, that they would suffer the same end as them.'*

Ibn Kathir supports this third sense with an ayah from later in this same sūrah: *"And We made them a precedent, and an example to later generations"* (43:56).

## The unchanging way of Allah

Ibn Kathir closes the passage with two further ayat that name the principle underneath it: *"this has been the way of Allah in dealing with His servants"* (40:85), and *"and you will not find any change in the way of Allah"* (33:62).

That is where his commentary on these four ayat comes to rest. What happens between Allah and those who reject His messengers is not improvised case by case. There is a *sunnah* — an established practice of Allah with His servants — and Allah Himself says it does not change.

## Living it

**Do not read your comfort as approval.** The first reading of ayah 5 asks the transgressor whether he imagines he will be forgiven and not punished while he does not do as he has been commanded. That question is put to be answered honestly.

**Treat the Qur'an still reaching you as a mercy.** Qatadah's insight, which Ibn Kathir praises, is that the continued calling of a rejecting people was Allah's grace and mercy towards His creation — He kept sending it, in Qatadah's words, "for twenty years, or for as long as He willed." That the Reminder is still in your hands is that same grace.

**Never close the file on anyone.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's lesson is the most concrete demand in the passage: carry the message to everybody, and do not let a person's disbelief, irreligion, sin or transgression be your reason to stop.

**Expect to be laughed at, and do not let it stop you.** Ayah 7 tells the Prophet ﷺ that no prophet came to those communities without being mocked, and Ibn Kathir names the response Allah commands: patience.

**Look at how strength ends.** Ayah 8 measures the mighty of Makkah against people stronger in power who were destroyed, and the ayah Ibn Kathir cites alongside it calls people to travel the earth and see the end of those before them. Whatever power looks permanent — your own or someone else's — the example of the ancients has already passed away, and you will not find any change in the way of Allah.

passages.title: The Creator they acknowledge, and the traveller's prayer
passages.tafsir:
These ayat take the one thing the idolaters of Makkah would not deny — that Allah alone made the heavens and the earth — and walk it downwards, from the sky to the ground under their feet, to the rain, to the animals they ride, until the argument arrives at the saddle of a camel and turns into a prayer on the lips of a traveller. What holds ayat 9–14 together is that single downward movement: an admission (9), the evidence they live inside every day (10–12), and then the response that admission should produce — words of glorification when you mount your ride, and the memory that the last journey is to Allah Himself (13–14).

## The admission they could not avoid (ayah 9)

Ibn Kathir opens by placing the question exactly: Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ that if he were to ask "these idolators who associate others with Allah and worship others besides Him" who created the heavens and the earth, they would answer without hesitation.

And notice the answer the Qur'an puts in their mouths: *"The All-Mighty, the All-Knower created them"* — al-ʿAzīz, al-ʿAlīm. They do not merely concede a vague first cause; they concede a Creator described by might and knowledge. Ibn Kathir draws out the contradiction plainly: "they will admit that the Creator of all that is Allah Alone, with no partner or associate, yet they still worship others — idols and false gods — alongside Him."

That is the hinge of the whole passage. The problem was never that they lacked information about who made the world. The problem was that their worship did not follow their own knowledge. Everything from ayah 10 onward is Allah pressing on that gap — not with new facts, but with familiar ones.

## The evidence underfoot (ayah 10)

**"Who has made for you the earth like a bed."** The word is *mahd*, which the translators render both as a bed laid out and as a cradle. Ibn Kathir explains it as "smooth, stable and firm, so that you can travel about in it, and stand on it and sleep and walk about." Then he adds the detail that turns stability into a marvel rather than an assumption: it is "created above water, but He has strengthened it with the mountains, lest it should shake." What feels to us like the most ordinary fact in existence — that the ground does not move — is in fact something held steady for us.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the cradle image: "the comfort provided by the earth is that of a cradle." A cradle is not flat; it is shaped, and it rocks a child into rest. Maʿārif then makes an important interpretive note — the earth's "apparent look of being a plain floor does not negate its being spherical." The Qur'an here is describing how the earth *serves* you, not delivering a geometry lesson; *mahd* speaks of comfort and fitness for human life.

**"And has made for you roads therein."** Ibn Kathir: "paths between the mountains and the valleys" — and their purpose, "in order that you may find your way," means "in your journeys from city to city, region to region, land to land." Hold on to this. Travel has now entered the passage, and it will not leave; by ayah 13 the whole discourse is about a man on the back of a mount.

## Water in measure, and the argument for resurrection (ayah 11)

**"Who sends down water from the sky in due measure"** — *bi-qadar*, in a determined amount. Ibn Kathir explains the measure precisely: "according to what is sufficient for your crops, fruits and drinking water for yourselves and your cattle." Rain is not simply generous; it is calibrated. Too little would starve them, too much would drown them; what falls is what the crops, the fruit, the people and the herds require.

Then: **"We revive a dead land therewith."** Ibn Kathir describes a barren land, "for when the water comes to it, it is stirred (to life), and it swells and puts forth every lovely kind (of growth)."

And now the passage does something quietly decisive. It does not stop at gratitude for rain; it turns the rain into a proof. As Ibn Kathir puts it, "by referring to the revival of the earth, Allah draws attention to how He will bring bodies back to life on the Day of Resurrection, after they have been dead." Hence the closing words of the ayah: **"and even so you will be brought forth."**

This is why the passage matters so much for anyone who has ever found resurrection hard to imagine. The reply is not an argument from abstraction. It is a pointing finger: look at a land that is barren and dead, and see what happens to it when the water comes. The One who stirs that ground back to life and makes it swell with growth is drawing your attention, says Ibn Kathir, to what He will do with bodies that have died.

## Pairs, ships and cattle (ayah 12)

**"Who has created all the pairs."** Ibn Kathir reads *al-azwāj* broadly: "of everything that grows in the earth, all kinds of plants, crops, fruits, flowers, etc., and all different kinds of animals." Creation comes to us in matched, paired kinds — a design running through the living world.

**"And has appointed for you ships"** — Ibn Kathir glosses *al-fulk* simply as ships "or vessels" — **"and cattle on which you ride."** Of the cattle he says Allah "has subjugated them to you and made it easy for you to eat their meat, drink their milk and ride on their backs."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this ayah up in a way that reaches straight into modern life. It observes that man has two kinds of transport: "those vehicles which are made by man himself, and two the animals in whose creation human effort is not involved at all." *Fulk* covers the first category — "all kinds of man-made vehicles" — and *anʿām* the second, "all the animals used for riding."

Why is the animal a blessing? Maʿārif answers with an image anyone who has seen livestock will recognise: despite these animals "being many times stronger than man, Allah Almighty has made them so submissive to him that even a child leads them to wherever he wants" by a halter or nose-string. The strength is theirs; the docility is a gift.

And the man-made vehicle? Maʿārif is emphatic that it is no less a favour from Allah — "right from the bicycles to the aeroplanes and the space-crafts" — "because they are, though, made by man apparently, there is no other than Allah Taʿālā who has provided man with ability and techniques to manufacture them." It is Allah "who has endowed the human intellect with the power that moulds iron like wax. And besides, all the raw materials used in their manufacturing and their properties are direct creations of Allah Almighty."

So a believer boarding a plane in the twenty-first century is standing exactly where the ayah places him. The engineering is human; the intellect that engineered it, the iron, and the properties of the iron are not.

## The traveller's words (ayah 13)

**"So that you may sit firmly on their backs."** Ibn Kathir glosses *li-tastawū* as to "sit comfortably and securely" — settled, balanced, at ease on the mount.

But the sitting is not the goal. The purpose clause continues: **"and then remember the favour of your Lord"** — the favour, says Ibn Kathir, "whereby these animals are subjugated to you." The moment of comfort is meant to trigger the memory of the Giver. And then the remembering is given words to say:

> **"Glory to Him Who has subjected this to us, and we could have never had it. And verily, to our Lord we indeed are to return."**

On *wa mā kunnā lahu muqrinīn* — "we could have never had it" — Ibn Kathir explains: "if it were not for the fact that Allah has subjugated these things to us, we could never have done this by our own strength." He then names four early authorities who all said the same thing of this phrase — **Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, As-Suddī and Ibn Zayd**: "We could not have done this ourselves."

Maʿārif applies that confession to modern transport with force: "if Allah Taʿālā had not created their raw materials, or had not endowed them with their particular properties, or had not endowed the human intellect with capability to discover those properties, even the whole universe, acting together in unison, could not have produced these vehicles."

**How to say it.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that saying these words on mounting a transport "was the practice of the Holy Prophet ﷺ according to many narrations." It then gives, citing Qurtubi, the preferred (*mustaḥabb*) sequence as stated by Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him):

1. Say **Bismillāh** as you place your first foot on the animal or the vehicle.
2. Once you have settled yourself on it, say **al-ḥamdu lillāh**.
3. Then say the words of this ayah: *Subḥāna alladhī sakhkhara lanā hādhā wa mā kunnā lahu muqrinīn, wa innā ilā rabbinā la-munqalibūn.*

Maʿārif adds, again from Qurtubi, that according to some reports the Prophet ﷺ would follow this with a further supplication:

> "O Allah, You are my companion in the journey, and my substitute for my family. O Allah, I seek Your refuge from the sufferings of the journey, and from coming back in a sad situation, and from a bad state of being after a good one, and from a bad scenario appearing to me about my family and my belongings."

And in one narration these words are added:

> "O Allah, there is no god but You. I have done wrong to myself; so forgive me. Surely, no one can forgive the sins, but You alone."

Look at what this prayer actually covers: the road itself, the family and property left behind, the fear of returning worse than you left, and finally your own sin. The traveller is exposed on every side, and the du'a names every side.

## The last journey (ayah 14)

The traveller's words end where the passage ends: **"And surely to our Lord we will all return."** Ibn Kathir: "We will return to Him after our death, and our ultimate destination is with Him."

Then he shows that this is a settled Qur'anic method — the everyday thing is made to point at the eternal one. "In this Ayah, mention of earthly journeys draws attention to the journey of the Hereafter," exactly as elsewhere the mention of earthly provision points to provision for the Hereafter — *"And take a provision for the journey, but the best provision is the Taqwa"* (2:197) — and the mention of earthly clothing points to the clothing of the Hereafter — *"and as an adornment; and the raiment of the Taqwa, that is better"* (7:26).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion: "every time a man embarks on a journey, he should think of his last arduous journey to the Hereafter also, which one has to undertake in all circumstances; and the only way to make it easy is to have a vehicle of good deeds."

It is a striking closing image. In this world you choose a mount and Allah makes it carry you. In the journey that no one is excused from, your mount is what you have done.

## Living it

**Do not use a blessing absent-mindedly.** Commenting on "then recall the favour of your Lord," Maʿārif says a sensible and alert person "should not display negligence, carelessness" or act as though he has no need of divine help "while enjoying the blessings of the Actual Benefactor"; rather he should acknowledge that it is a reward from Allah Almighty, "obliging him to be grateful and to display his impotence and humility."

**This is the dividing line.** Maʿārif states it directly: the difference between an infidel and a Muʼmin is that the former "uses the good things of this world carelessly and negligently, while the Mu'min cognizant of the blessings of Allah bows his head to Allah Almighty in humility." Not different cars — a different heart in the same car.

**Ordinary life can be turned into worship.** Because of this, says Maʿārif, "the Qur'an and hadith have taught supplications for patience, steadfastness and gratefulness, and if anyone makes a habit of supplicating those prayers in his daily life while getting up, sitting down, walking about, etc., then all his (or hers) permissible activities turn into acts of worship." Maʿārif points the reader to two collections of such supplications: *Al-Ḥiṣn al-Ḥaṣīn* of ʿAllāmah Ibn al-Jazarī and *Munājāt-e-Maqbūl* of Maulānā Thānawī.

## The passage in one line

They already know Who made the world (9); He has spread the ground, sent the rain, paired the creation and tamed the mounts (10–12); so when you settle into your seat, let your mouth say what your knowledge already admits — *glory to the One who subjected this to us* — and remember that this road ends, and the road to your Lord does not (13–14).

passages.title: Assigning daughters to the Most Compassionate
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat take up one claim the idolaters of Makkah made — that the angels are Allah's daughters — and dismantle it from several sides at once. What holds the passage together is a single method: Allah does not merely deny the claim, He holds it up against the claimants' own words, their own feelings, and their own admitted ignorance, until it collapses under its own weight. Ayah 15 states the charge, ayah 16 turns it into a stinging question, ayat 17–18 expose it using the accusers' own reaction to daughters, and ayah 19 demands their evidence and warns that their answer is being written down.

## A pattern of dividing things up

Ibn Kathir begins by placing ayah 15 inside a habit these people already had. They were in the business of assigning shares. He points to Sūrat al-Anʿām, where Allah describes how they devoted some of their cattle to their false gods and some to Allah: "This is for Allah" — according to their claim — "and this is for our partners." And then, as that ayah goes on to say, the share of their partners never reached Allah, while the share of Allah found its way to their partners. Allah's verdict there: "Evil is the way they judge!" (6:136).

Ibn Kathir's point is that ayah 15 exposes the same instinct working on a far graver scale. Having divided the harvest and the herds, they went on to divide offspring. Of the two kinds — sons and daughters — they assigned to Him the one they themselves rated, in Ibn Kathir's words, "the worst and least valuable (in their eyes)." He brings the Qur'an's own summary of that arithmetic: "Is it for you the males and for Him the females? That indeed is a division most unfair!" (53:21–22).

So the passage is not addressing an abstract theological error. It is addressing people who kept the better share for themselves in every transaction, and did it even here.

## "A part of Him" — the force of the word *juzʾ*

The most striking thing in ayah 15 is the word Allah chooses. He does not say they attributed *offspring* to Him. He says: **وَجَعَلُوا لَهُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِ جُزْءًا** — they assigned to Him, out of His own servants, a **juzʾ**: a part, a portion, a piece. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the phrase, "And they have attributed to Him [that He is composed of parts] and that too out of His slaves."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this out carefully. *Juzʾ* here means offspring, "because the polytheists used to say that angels are daughters of Allah." But by using the word "parts" instead of "offspring," the Qur'an points out the fallacy of their claim "on pure logical ground." The reasoning runs like this: a son is a part of his father. So to say Allah has offspring is to say Allah has parts. But — and this is the rule Maʿārif ul Qurʼān rests on — "it is a rule of logic that an entity that consists of parts is dependent upon its parts for its full existence." A thing made of pieces needs its pieces in order to be whole.

Follow that to its end and you have said that Allah is dependent on His offspring, "which is obviously impossible." Dependence of any kind, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is a negation of the Divine Majesty — it is out of the question where Allah is concerned. He is not assembled. He has no components on which His being rests. So the claim does not merely insult Him; it destroys the very idea of a deity worthy of worship. One word, *juzʾ*, does all of that work.

The ayah closes: **إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَكَفُورٌ** — in Ibn Kathir's text, "Verily, man is indeed a manifest ingrate!" Ingratitude is the right diagnosis, because everything they were dividing up — the tilth, the cattle, the children — came from Him in the first place.

## Ayah 16: the question that cannot be answered

**أَمِ اتَّخَذَ مِمَّا يَخْلُقُ بَنَاتٍ وَأَصْفَاكُم بِالْبَنِينَ** — "Or has He taken daughters out of what He has created, and He has *selected* for you sons?"

Ibn Kathir calls this "a denunciation of them in the strongest terms." The question is not asked to gather information; it is asked so they will hear how it sounds. Notice its shape: out of everything He creates, He supposedly kept for Himself the category they dread, and *selected* them — chose, preferred, set aside — for the category they want. Said aloud, it answers itself.

## Ayat 17–18: their own faces convict them

Then comes the evidence, and it is devastating because it costs no argument at all. Allah simply describes what happens in one of their homes on the day a daughter is born.

**وَإِذَا بُشِّرَ أَحَدُهُم بِمَا ضَرَبَ لِلرَّحْمَٰنِ مَثَلًا ظَلَّ وَجْهُهُ مُسْوَدًّا وَهُوَ كَظِيمٌ** — "And if one of them is informed of the news of that which he sets forth as a parable to the Most Gracious, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with grief."

Ibn Kathir explains the scene plainly: one of these people is given the news that there has been born to him one of those which he attributes to Allah — a daughter — and "he hates this news and it depresses and overwhelms him so much that he keeps away from people because he feels so ashamed." Notice the detail of him withdrawing from company: the grief is not private sorrow but public humiliation. Then Ibn Kathir puts Allah's question: **so how can they dislike that so much and yet they attribute it to Allah?**

Two things in the wording deepen the wound. First, the ayah uses **بُشِّرَ** — the verb of *good news*, the announcement a man is congratulated over; the birth is reported as glad tidings, and then the face goes dark, and the gap between the two is the whole indictment. Second, the name used for Allah through this passage is **الرَّحْمَٰن**, the Most Gracious. It is to the Most Gracious that they assign what makes their own faces dark with shame.

Ayah 18 continues the questioning: **أَوَمَن يُنَشَّأُ فِي الْحِلْيَةِ وَهُوَ فِي الْخِصَامِ غَيْرُ مُبِينٍ** — "A creature who is brought up in adornments, and who in dispute cannot make itself clear?"

It matters here who is speaking and to whom. Ibn Kathir has already said that daughters were the share these people considered the worst and least valuable *in their eyes*, and he explains ayah 18 in that same register — women "are regarded as lacking something, which they make up for with jewelry and adornments from the time of childhood onwards, and when there is a dispute, they cannot speak up and defend themselves clearly" — before closing the same rhetorical loop he closed a moment earlier: *so how can this be attributed to Allah?*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws two side points out of ayah 18 in passing:

- **On adornment.** The phrase "grown up in ornaments" tells us that the use of ornaments and adornment in accordance with the Sharīʿah is permissible for women — and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, there is consensus on this issue. At the same time, it adds, the manner of speech indicates that becoming so involved in adornment that one is busy in it the whole day long is not proper: it is "not only a symptom of one's being short-sighted, but also a cause of it."
- **On the second half.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads "and who cannot express themselves in debate clearly" as a statement about the general case, and says so explicitly: it reflects that a great majority of women do not have the same ability as men to express their feelings clearly, which makes it difficult, in argumentation, to prove their own contention and refute another's arguments in a clear manner. But — in its own words — "this applies to the majority. If some women are eloquent in their speech and excel even men in this regard, it does not go against this verse, because the rule applies to the majority, and not to every single individual."

## Ayah 19: servants, not daughters — and where is the evidence?

**وَجَعَلُوا الْمَلَائِكَةَ الَّذِينَ هُمْ عِبَادُ الرَّحْمَٰنِ إِنَاثًا** — "And they make females the angels who themselves are servants of the Most Gracious."

Before Allah rejects the claim, the ayah states what the angels actually are: *ʿibād al-Raḥmān*, the servants of the Most Gracious. Ibn Kathir's comment on the first part is brief and exact — "that is what they believe about them" — and then, he says, Allah denounces them for that:

**أَشَهِدُوا خَلْقَهُمْ** — "Did they witness their creation?" Ibn Kathir: "did they see Allah creating them as females?" This is the demand for evidence, and it is the heart of the ayah. They were filing a report on beings they had never laid eyes on, about a moment of creation no human attended — and, as Ibn Kathir says elsewhere in this passage, with "no proof, evidence or permission from Allah."

**سَتُكْتَبُ شَهَادَتُهُمْ وَيُسْأَلُونَ** — "Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned." Ibn Kathir explains both halves plainly: their testimony will be recorded concerning that, and they will be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection. He adds: "This is a stern warning and a serious threat."

There is a quiet courtroom shape to the ayah worth seeing. *Did they witness?* — the challenge to a witness. *Their testimony will be recorded* — the statement taken down. *And they will be questioned* — the questioning, deferred to the Day of Resurrection. They spoke as though giving evidence about Allah and His angels; very well, the evidence has been entered, and they will be asked about it.

## The larger error, and what it asks of us

Commenting on this stretch of the sūrah, Ibn Kathir sets out how many errors these people managed to combine: they attributed offspring to Allah — exalted and sanctified be He far above that; they claimed He chose daughters rather than sons, and made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Gracious, female; and they worshipped them with no proof, evidence or permission from Allah, on the basis of "mere opinion, whims and desires, imitation of their elders and forefathers, and pure ignorance." Against all of that stands what the command has been from the time Allah first sent Messengers and revealed Books — to worship Him alone with no partner or associate — which Ibn Kathir anchors in the ayah: "And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger (proclaiming): 'Worship Allah, and avoid all false deities'" (16:36).

Three things to carry away.

**Guard how you speak about Allah.** Every error in this passage began as speech about Him that nobody had authority to make. The test ayah 19 sets is simple: *did you witness it, or do you have proof, evidence or permission from Allah?* If neither, silence is safer than a sentence you will be questioned about.

**Do not repeat the division.** These were people who gave Allah the share they valued least and kept the better one — in their tilth, in their cattle, and finally in their beliefs. It is worth asking honestly what share of our time, wealth and attention we assign to Him, and whether it is the portion we would want for ourselves.

**Beware of inherited belief.** Ibn Kathir names imitation of elders and forefathers among the things their worship rested on. A belief that has never been examined is not thereby true; it is only unexamined.

And there is a tenderness in the passage a reader should not miss. The birth of a daughter is announced in ayah 17 with the language of *good news*, and the shame belongs entirely to the man whose face darkens. Allah reports his reaction not to endorse it but to hold it against him — *so how can they dislike that so much and yet they attribute it to Allah?* A community that has read these ayat has been shown plainly how Allah regards that reaction.

passages.title: Their two excuses: Allah's will and the forefathers' way
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat put two excuses of the Makkan idolaters on trial and dismantle both.

## What holds the passage together

Two sentences the idolaters said, and Allah's reply to each. In ayah 20 they say: *"If it had been the will of the Most Gracious, we should not have worshipped them"* — the excuse of destiny. In ayah 22 they say: *"We found our fathers following a certain way and religion, and we guide ourselves by their footsteps"* — the excuse of inheritance. Between the two, ayah 21 asks the question that exposes both: **do you have a Book from Allah that says so?** Ayat 23–25 then widen the lens: this is not a Makkan quirk. Every warner sent to every town met the same sentence from the same kind of people, and the passage closes by pointing at what became of them.

Ibn Kathir places ayah 20 under the heading *Condemnation of the Idolators' attribution of Offspring to Allah*, and then gathers ayat 21–25 together under a second heading: *The Idolators have no Proof*. That second heading names the thread running through the rest of the passage — **worship without evidence, defended by two arguments that are not arguments at all.**

## Who is "them"?

Ayah 20 says "we should not have worshipped *them*" without naming them. Ibn Kathir supplies the reference in his gloss on the ayah itself: what they meant was, *'if Allah had willed, He would have prevented us from worshipping these idols which are images of the angels who are the daughters of Allah; He knows about this and He approves of it.'*

So the idols were, in their own belief, images of the angels — whom they took to be Allah's daughters. That belief has just been taken apart in the ayat immediately before. Ibn Kathir recalls that these were people who devoted some of their cattle to their false gods and some to Allah (as described in 6:136); who assigned to Him, out of sons and daughters, what was in their own eyes the least valuable — daughters — while keeping sons for themselves, which the Qur'an calls "a division most unfair" (53:21–22); and who made the angels, "who themselves are servants of the Most Gracious," female. Ibn Kathir notes how sharply this exposes them: when one of these men was given the news that a daughter had been born to him, he hated the news, and it depressed and overwhelmed him so much that he kept away from people out of shame — *so how can they dislike that so much and yet they attribute it to Allah?*

That is the belief being defended in ayah 20 by an appeal to the will of Allah.

## The first excuse: "If it had been the will of the Most Gracious"

Read their sentence as Ibn Kathir unpacks it, and you hear what they actually meant: *if Allah had wanted to, He would have stopped us worshipping these idols. He has not stopped us. He knows about it, and He approves of it.* They are not making a philosophical observation about divine power. They are claiming Allah's silent endorsement — turning what He permits to occur into a licence.

Ibn Kathir lays out how many errors they piled into one sentence. By saying this, he writes, "they combined several types of error":

1. **They attributed offspring to Allah** — exalted and sanctified be He, far above that.
2. **They claimed He chose daughters rather than sons**, and made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Gracious, female.
3. **They worshipped them with no proof, evidence or permission from Allah.** It was based on mere opinion, whims and desires, imitation of their elders and forefathers, and pure ignorance. And then, says Ibn Kathir, "they used Allah's decree as an excuse, and this reasoning betrayed their ignorance."
4. **Allah denounced them for this in the strongest terms**, because from the time He first sent Messengers and revealed Books, the command was to worship Him alone with no partner or associate, and it was forbidden to worship anything other than Him.

That fourth point is the heart of the refutation, and Ibn Kathir supports it with two ayat. The first: *"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger: 'Worship Allah, and avoid all false deities'"* (16:36). The second is from this very sūrah, a few ayat ahead: *"And ask those of Our Messengers whom We sent before you: 'Did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Gracious?'"* (43:45).

The logic is worth slowing down over. Their appeal is to what Allah allowed to happen. Ibn Kathir answers it with what Allah *commanded* — a command that has never varied since the first Messenger was sent. If Allah's allowing an act were the same as His approving it, He would not have sent to every single nation a Messenger saying *worship Allah, and avoid all false deities*. The idolaters' argument is therefore refuted not by any dispute over the divine will, but by the messengers standing in every generation saying plainly: *do not do this*. A man who is told plainly not to do something, does it anyway, and then says "well, I was allowed to" has not answered the messenger. He has changed the subject.

And this excuse is one the guilty reach for only after the fact. No one uses it to decide what to do; they use it to explain away what they have already done. Ibn Kathir's phrase is exact — it is a reasoning that "betrayed their ignorance."

## Allah's verdict on it: two short clauses

*"They have no knowledge whatsoever of that. They do nothing but lie!"*

**"They have no knowledge whatsoever of that."** Ibn Kathir explains: no knowledge "of the truth of what they say and the arguments they put forward." Not merely that they are wrong — they have nothing that even counts as evidence. Their claim about the angels, their claim about Allah's approval: all of it is assertion.

**"They do nothing but lie!"** Ibn Kathir renders it plainly: "they tell lies and fabricate untruths." The sentence they offered as a defence is classified, in Allah's own verdict on it, as fabrication.

Then a single line from Mujahid that reaches deeper than the argument itself: **"They do not appreciate the power of Allah."** Underneath the clever excuse is a small idea of Allah. A person who truly weighed Allah's power as Mujahid says these people failed to weigh it would never have thought to use Him as an alibi.

## Ayah 21: "Or have We given them a Book before this?"

The particle *am* ("or") turns the passage into cross-examination. Very well — if you claim Allah endorses your worship, produce His endorsement. Where is the scripture?

Ibn Kathir reads "before this" as **"before their idolatry"** — is there some earlier revelation they received, which they are now *holding fast* to? And "to which they are holding fast" he glosses as: "with regard to what they are doing."

The answer, Ibn Kathir says flatly, is: **"This is not the case."** He compares it to *"Or have We revealed to them an authority, which speaks of that which they have been associating with Him?"* (30:35) — "meaning, that did not happen."

The question is not rhetorical decoration. It sets the standard for what may be worshipped and how: **a text from Allah, or nothing.** Whatever else the idolaters could produce, they could not produce that.

## Ayah 22: "Nay — we found our fathers"

*Bal* — "nay," "rather" — cuts off the previous possibility and substitutes the real one. No Book. What they actually have is: *"We found our fathers following a certain way and religion (ummah), and we guide ourselves by their footsteps."*

Ibn Kathir states the verdict before the detail: **they have no grounds for their belief in idolatry apart from the fact that they are imitating their fathers and forefathers** who were following a certain *ummah* or way — that is, a religion.

Two words carry the ayah.

**Ummah.** Here it does not mean a people or community but a *way, a religion*. Ibn Kathir supports the usage from elsewhere in the Qur'an: *"And verily, this your religion (ummah) is one religion"* (23:52).

**Āthār — footsteps.** Ibn Kathir glosses *"and we by their footsteps"* as simply: **"behind them."** That is the whole of their religion in one word — positioned behind, walking where others walked. They never ask where the tracks lead or who first made them.

And notice their claim: *muhtadūn*, "we guide ourselves" — they do not say "we are imitators," they use the language of guidance itself. Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and devastating: **"This is their claim with no evidence."** Imitation dressed in the vocabulary of guidance is still imitation.

## Ayah 23: the same sentence, in every town

Then Allah widens the frame, and this is where the passage becomes something more than a report on Makkah. Ibn Kathir puts it exactly: what these people say **"was already said by those who were like them among the nations of the past who disbelieved in the Messengers. Their hearts and their words are similar."** He supports it with *"Likewise, no Messenger came to those before them but they said: 'A sorcerer or a madman!' Have they transmitted this saying to these? Nay, they are themselves a people transgressing beyond bounds!"* (51:52–53). No one passed the script down; the same disease produces the same speech.

Two details in ayah 23 repay attention.

**"To any town" — every warner, everywhere.** *"We sent not a warner before you to any town (people) but the luxurious ones among them said..."* The pattern is universal, which means the Prophet ﷺ is meeting nothing that the warners before him did not meet.

**"The luxurious ones among them" — *mutrafūhā*.** Allah does not say the poor or the ignorant led the resistance; the ayah names the luxurious ones, the ones the existing order had been good to. They are precisely the people with the most to lose if the inherited way turns out to be false. The excuse of the forefathers is very often, underneath, the excuse of the comfortable.

**One word changes.** In ayah 22 the Makkans say *muhtadūn* — "we guide ourselves." In ayah 23 the earlier nations say *muqtadūn* — "we will indeed follow their footsteps." The claim to guidance has fallen away; what is left is the bare fact of following. Both sentences do the same work; the second does it with less self-flattery.

## Ayah 24: the question that ends the argument

The warner — every warner, in every one of those towns — answers with a single question: *"Even if I bring you better guidance than that which you found your fathers following?"*

This is the fairest question that can be asked of someone defending an inherited practice, and it concedes a great deal. It does not sneer at the fathers or demand that their memory be insulted. It only asks: **if what I bring is more guided, will you take it?** Anyone genuinely seeking guidance must say yes; the whole point of following the fathers was that they were thought to be on the right path, so the moment a better path is shown the reason for following collapses.

Their reply refuses to engage at all: *"Verily, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."* Not "prove it." Not "show us." Ibn Kathir draws out what this exposes: **even if they were convinced of the truth of what was brought to them, they would not follow it** — "because of their evil intentions and their arrogance towards the truth and its people."

That is the real diagnosis of the passage. The forefathers were never the reason. They were the cover story. Underneath, in Ibn Kathir's words, were evil intentions and arrogance — arrogance not only towards the truth itself, but towards the people who carry it.

## Ayah 25: "So We took revenge on them"

Ibn Kathir explains: **"on the disbelieving nations, by inflicting various kinds of punishments, as Allah has described in the stories of those nations."** The *fā'* at the start — "so," "then" — makes the punishment follow directly on the refusal just recorded. The argument ended; the consequence followed.

Then the passage turns to the reader: *"then see what was the end of those who denied."* And Ibn Kathir's gloss on it is quietly complete: **"see what became of them, how they were destroyed and how Allah saved the believers."**

The ruins are only half of what the eye is being directed to. The other half is the small, mocked, out-argued group who held to what the warner brought — and whom Allah saved.

## Living it

**Never use the decree as a defence.** The idolaters' sentence — "if Allah hadn't willed it, we wouldn't have done it" — is still on people's lips today, applied to sins rather than idols. Ibn Kathir's answer stands: from the time Allah first sent Messengers and revealed Books, the command was to worship Him alone and to avoid false deities. That an act was possible never made it commanded, and never made it approved.

**Ask ayah 24's question of your own practice.** *Even if better guidance came?* Inherited custom is not the enemy here; refusing to test it is. Where a family or cultural practice matches what Allah revealed, keep it gratefully. Where it collides with revealed guidance, ayah 22 has already told you what "we found our fathers doing it" is worth as evidence — Ibn Kathir's verdict on exactly that sentence was: "This is their claim with no evidence."

**Watch what comfort does to hearing.** Ayah 23 names the luxurious ones as the ones who dug in. It is worth asking honestly which truths one resists, and whether the resistance is really about evidence — or about what accepting it would cost.

**Take the consolation.** If you call people to something true and are met with "this is how we have always done it," ayah 23 tells you that no warner before you was spared that answer either. And ayah 25 tells you how those stories ended — both halves of it: how the deniers were destroyed, and how Allah saved the believers.

passages.title: Abraham's disavowal and its abandoned legacy
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat put Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in front of the Quraysh as a mirror. They boasted of descending from him and of taking their religion from him — so Allah recalls the one sentence that defined him: a clean break with the worship of his own father and people, and the word he left behind for his descendants to come home to. Ayat 29 and 30 then show what those descendants did with it: generations of comfortable enjoyment, and then, when the truth finally arrived in the person of a clear Messenger, the answer "this is magic."

## The argument these ayat are answering

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. In the verses just before, Allah had made clear that the *mushrikīn* (idolaters) of Arabia had no argument for their *shirk* (associating partners with Allah) except that they were carrying on the customs of their forefathers. And clinging to inherited custom against logical and historical proof, as Maʿārif puts it, is far from truth and justice.

So the passage takes their own logic and turns it on them. Very well — if you insist on following your ancestors, why not follow the noblest ancestor you have? Ibn Kathir notes that Quraysh were descended from Ibrahim and claimed to have taken their religion from him. Maʿārif presses the point twice over: Ibrahim was not only a believer in *tawḥīd* (Allah's absolute oneness) who urged his children to hold to it — his whole life is itself the refutation of blind ancestor-following. When prophethood came to him, all his people were idolaters following the customs of *their* forefathers, and he did not follow them. He announced his dissociation from them on the strength of positive proof.

## "I am free of what you worship" (ayah 26)

Ibn Kathir introduces the speaker with full weight: Allah's servant, His Messenger, His close Friend, the leader of the monotheists and the father of all subsequent Prophets. This is not a marginal voice. By the Quraysh's own account, he is the ancestor they descend from and the source they claimed their religion came from.

Notice who he addresses: **his father and his people**. The nearest tie and the widest circle at once — nothing is exempted for the sake of family feeling.

The key word is *barāʼ*. The renderings before us give it as "I am innocent of what you worship" and "I disown that which you worship" — and both are needed to feel it. It is not a mild "I personally don't do that." It is a declaration of having no part in the thing, being clear of it, cutting the rope.

Maʿārif draws out exactly this and turns it into a rule of conduct: **if someone lives among people who are misguided or engaged in bad deeds, and his silence about their conduct could be read as agreement with them, it is not enough for him to correct only his own beliefs and deeds — he must disown theirs as well.** That is precisely what Ibrahim did. He did not merely make his belief and practice visibly different; he disowned their belief and deeds *vocally*.

## The one exception (ayah 27)

Having swept away everything they worship, ayah 27 keeps back one: "except the One Who originated me" — *al-ladhī faṭaranī*, which Ibn Kathir renders "Him Who created me."

Look at the reason embedded in the exception. Ibrahim does not say "except the greatest of the gods" or "except the one my heart prefers." The ground he stands on is creation itself: the only being with any claim on my worship is the One who brought me into existence. Everything else in the room owes its existence to Someone; only the Originator does not.

Then: "and He will surely guide me." He says it in the future tense, at the exact moment he has cut himself off from his father, his people and their whole religious world. He is not left standing in the open with no direction. Having chosen the One who made him, he trusts that this One will keep showing him the way. The confidence is not in his own reasoning but in Allah's guidance.

## The word he left behind (ayah 28)

"And he made it a word lasting among his offspring, that they may turn back."

**What is "it"?** Ibn Kathir is explicit: the Word means the worship of Allah alone with no partner or associate, together with the denunciation of every god apart from Him — that is, *lā ilāha illa-llāh*. Ibrahim left this word as an example to be followed by those of his progeny whom Allah guided.

The early authorities are unanimous here. Ibn Kathir cites ʿIkrimah, Mujahid, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others on this ayah: "This means *lā ilāha illa-llāh*, and there are still those among his offspring who say it." A similar view is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Zayd said "the word of Islam" — which, as Ibn Kathir observes, comes to the same thing the group said.

**"That they may turn back"** — Ibn Kathir explains: that they may come back to this word. The verb is one of *returning*, not of arriving somewhere new. That is the mercy hidden in the ayah: a descendant who has drifted into idolatry is not being invited to a foreign creed but called home to what his own forefather left him.

**A word that outlived him.** Maʿārif adds the historical detail that makes ayah 28 ache. Ibrahim did not keep *tawḥīd* to himself; he pressed it on his posterity, and as a result a great many of his descendants held to it. In Makkah and its surroundings there were still blessed souls, right up to the coming of the Prophet ﷺ, who had remained steadfast on the original religion of Ibrahim. So the word was never entirely extinguished in that city — it survived in a scattered few, while the crowd around the Kaʿbah, the descendants of the man who built his life on *lā ilāha illa-llāh*, had swapped it for idols.

## Raising children on the word: a prophetic practice

Maʿārif takes a clear practical duty from this ayah: it is among the obligations of a Muslim to strive his utmost to set his children on the correct religion and to have them live by it throughout their lives. It cites the Qur'an's report that Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, likewise instructed his sons shortly before his death to hold firm to the correct faith. This is the consistent practice of the prophets — so exerting one's best effort to reform the character and conduct of one's children is a religious necessity, not an optional extra.

The means vary with the situation, Maʿārif notes, but it quotes Shaikh ʿAbd al-Wahhāb ash-Shaʿrānī, in his book *Laṭāʼif ul-Minan wal-Akhlāq*, that the most effective means of all for the good of one's offspring in matters of religion is that **the parents should pray to Allah regularly to make them true, practising Muslims**. Maʿārif then laments how commonly parents neglect this easy way — and how visibly they suffer the results.

There is something quietly moving in placing this beside ayah 28. Ibrahim's greatest bequest was not property. It was a sentence, planted in his line, that kept surfacing long after him.

## "Rather, I gave these and their fathers enjoyment" (ayah 29)

The *bal* — "rather," "nay but" — swings the passage from Ibrahim's line to the men standing in front of the Prophet ﷺ. And the speaker changes: it is now Allah Himself, in the first person. "I gave to these" — Ibn Kathir: meaning the idolaters — "and their fathers," meaning, he explains, **they lived a long life in their misguidance**.

That is the sting. Their long, comfortable run was not an oversight and it was not a verdict in their favour. It was Allah granting them enjoyment. Length of days in misguidance had let them mistake continuity for correctness: our fathers lived this way for generations and nothing happened.

But the sentence has a limit built into it: *until* the truth came to them, and a clear Messenger. Ibn Kathir explains "a Messenger making things clear" to mean **his message is clear and his warning is clear** — no ambiguity left for anyone to hide behind. Note the pairing: what arrived was both a truth and a man; a message and a messenger who made it plain. After that, the enjoyment is over as an excuse.

## "This is magic, and we disbelieve in it" (ayah 30)

Ayah 30 gives their answer, and it is not a request for evidence. Ibn Kathir's reading of it: **they were arrogant and stubborn, and they pushed him away out of disbelief, envy and transgression.**

Notice what that leaves out. Ibn Kathir does not describe their reply as confusion or honest doubt; he describes a posture. And ayah 29 has just ruled out the excuse of not understanding — what came to them was the truth, carried by a Messenger whose message and warning were clear. So "this is magic" is a label placed on the truth rather than an examination of it, and "we disbelieve in it" is a refusal stated outright.

## Two disavowals, facing each other

The passage is built on a symmetry worth pausing over. Ibrahim declares in ayah 26: *innanī barāʼun mimmā taʿbudūn* — I am free of what you worship. His descendants declare in ayah 30: *innā bihi kāfirūn* — we disbelieve in it. The same emphatic form, the same public confidence, aimed at opposite objects. Ibrahim disowned falsehood and Allah made him, in Ibn Kathir's words, the leader of the monotheists and the father of all subsequent Prophets; they disowned the truth and thereby cut themselves off from the very word their forefather had left them, in the very city where blessed souls had kept it alive until the Prophet ﷺ came.

That is what makes this passage a single unit. Ayah 26 to 28: a man breaks with his people to hold one word, and plants it in his line so they can always come back. Ayah 29 to 30: his line has the word within reach, is given generations of ease, is finally sent a Messenger who spells it out — and calls it sorcery.

## Living it

**Silence is not neutrality.** Where staying quiet among wrongdoing would be read as agreement, Maʿārif's lesson from ayah 26 applies: correcting your own belief and practice is not enough; the disowning has to be said, not only lived. This is about disowning the *belief and the deeds* — Ibrahim's words in ayah 26 name what they worship, not their persons.

**Inheritance is a word, not an estate.** Ayah 28 measures a life by what survives it. Work at putting your children on this religion, in whatever way fits them — and do not skip the means Maʿārif calls the most effective of all: asking Allah, regularly, to make them truly practising.

**A long comfortable run proves nothing.** Ayah 29 is Allah's own account of why the idolaters had been left alone so long. Uninterrupted ease is not a certificate of approval; it can simply be the enjoyment granted until the truth arrives.

**Test the claim, not the custom.** Quraysh had the prestige of descent from Ibrahim and lost everything that mattered about it. Ibrahim himself is the proof that ancestry is worth nothing without the word — and that a man with the word, standing alone against his whole people, can trust that Allah will guide him.

passages.title: Who distributes your Lord's mercy?
passages.tafsir:
This passage answers one objection: the Quraysh could accept neither that a man be a messenger at all, nor — once that was settled — that the man chosen be *this* man. If prophethood had to go to a human being, they said, let it go to somebody important. Ayat 31–35 are Allah's reply, and it moves in a single arc: you do not control the distribution of My mercy; you do not even control the distribution of your own daily bread; and the wealth you use as your measuring stick is so worthless to Me that I would have showered it on those who reject Me, were it not for the danger that people would then sell their faith to get it.

## The objection behind ayah 31

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The pagans of Arabia were not prepared, in the first place, to accept that a man could be a messenger of Allah at all — the Qur'an refers in many places to their objection that this man eats and drinks and walks about in the market places like any ordinary man. When it had been clarified that not only the Prophet ﷺ but all the prophets who came into this world were human beings, they advanced another argument: if prophethood had to be bestowed upon a human being, why was it not given to some wealthy man of high rank and position from Makkah or Ṭāʼif, instead of the Prophet ﷺ, who was not so wealthy?

That is the sting in **ayah 31**: *"Why is not this Qur'an sent down to some great man of the two towns?"* Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: why was this Qur'an not revealed to some man who was **great and prominent in their eyes**, from the two towns — that is, Makkah and aṭ-Ṭāʼif? This was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), ʿIkrimah, Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, Qatādah, as-Suddī and Ibn Zayd. Notice the qualifier Ibn Kathir uses: great *in their eyes*.

Several scholars of tafsir, Ibn Kathir reports, stated that by this the Quraysh meant al-Walīd bin al-Mughīrah and ʿUrwah bin Masʿūd ath-Thaqafī. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, records that according to some narrations they had proposed the names of al-Walīd ibn Mughīrah and ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah from Makkah, and ʿUrwah ibn Masʿūd Thaqafī, Ḥabīb ibn ʿAmr Thaqafī or Kinānah ibn ʿAbd Yālīl from Ṭāʼif. Ibn Kathir then adds that the apparent meaning of the wording is that what they meant was simply a great man from either of the two towns.

Read the ayat just before: Allah had given them and their fathers long enjoyment in their misguidance until the truth and a Messenger who made things clear came to them — and their response was, "This is magic, and we disbelieve therein." Ibn Kathir's comment on that response is unsparing: **"they were arrogant and stubborn, and they pushed him away out of disbelief, envy and transgression."** Ibn Kathir introduces the demand of ayah 31 in the same register — as an objection to what Allah had revealed to him. It is not an honest inquiry into credentials; it belongs to the same rejection.

And it comes from people who, as Ibn Kathir notes, were descended from Ibrāhīm and claimed to have taken their religion from him — Allah's servant, Messenger and close Friend, who disowned his people's worship of idols and left *lā ilāha illa Allah* as a word lasting among his offspring, that they might turn back to it.

## "Is it they who portion out the mercy of your Lord?" — ayah 32

The reply in **ayah 32** opens with a question that is really a rebuke: *a-hum yaqsimūna raḥmata rabbik* — "Is it *they* who would portion out the mercy of your Lord?" The pronoun stands at the front of the sentence, and it carries the force: *they?* These people? Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact: "the matter has nothing to do with them; it is for Allah to decide."

**What is "the mercy" here?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes it as prophethood itself: appointing someone as a prophet is a mercy from Allah which He bestows on the basis of His absolute wisdom and according to His exclusive discretion — for which He need not consult anyone, nor has anyone a right to interfere. Your advice is not to be sought before anyone is made a prophet; your intellect and understanding are too deficient to be entrusted with selecting suitable persons for that office.

Ibn Kathir supplies the positive side of the same point: **"Allah knows best where to direct His Message, and He does not reveal it except to the one who is the purest in heart and soul, and of the noblest descent."** The Quraysh were reading the wrong instrument: they measured by wealth and standing, while the criterion named here is purity of heart and soul, and nobility of descent. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes it explicit at ayah 35: some qualities and abilities are undoubtedly necessary for choosing someone as a prophet — but abundance of riches cannot be the basis of that choice; and those excellent qualities which are necessary for prophethood were found in the Prophet ﷺ to their perfection. Their objection is therefore false and baseless.

**Then comes the argument from the lesser to the greater.** The same verb of apportioning that was just denied to them is now claimed by Allah for Himself, with an emphatic pronoun of His own: *naḥnu qasamnā baynahum maʿīshatahum* — "**It is We** Who portion out between them their livelihood in this world." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic: how can you distribute among people an office as high as prophethood, when you have no ability to distribute something much lower and easier — your economy? Entrusted with that responsibility, you would not be able to manage it for a single day, and the whole system would simply collapse.

Ibn Kathir widens the frame: Allah differentiates among His creation in terms of **what He gives them of wealth, provision, intellect, understanding, and other visible and hidden strengths**. The inequality of ayah 32 — *"and We raised some of them above others in ranks"* — runs through every capacity a person has, not money alone.

## Why the ranks exist: so that some may employ others

The purpose clause is the heart of the ayah: *li-yattakhidha baʿḍuhum baʿḍan sukhriyyā* — "so that some may employ others in their work." Ibn Kathir reports the interpretation of as-Suddī and others: that some employ others in their work, **because one needs the other, and vice versa**. The dependence is mutual: not a class of masters over a class of servants, but a world stitched together by need.

**A system, not a scheme.** Allah in His infinite wisdom has devised a system for the world in which everybody is dependent on another for meeting his needs; bound in this mutual interdependence, all people end up fulfilling the needs of the whole society. The ayah has made it quite clear, Maʿārif argues, that Allah has *not* assigned the work of distributing livelihood to any human organisation or authority. All these functions rest with Allah. By making every person dependent upon another, an automatic system has been developed that resolves these issues — on one condition: that it is not hindered by unnatural factors like monopolies.

Maʿārif offers homely illustrations of what nature settles better than planning. Who should marry whom is arranged automatically through the natural system of personal inclinations. Human planning, however advanced, cannot take into account every element of human necessity. The economic system likewise is taken care of by Allah's wisdom and power: everybody knows in his heart what he wants to do and which job suits him — so that even a man who sweeps for a living can be happy in his work and proud of it.

**But not a licence.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful that this is no endorsement of capitalism as such. Unlike capitalism, Islam has not given individuals so much freedom that they may accumulate wealth by any means, lawful or unlawful, and deprive others of their livelihood. It has drawn a clear line between ḥalāl and ḥarām sources of income: it has totally prohibited usury or interest, speculative transactions, hoarding and gambling, and has levied zakāh, ʿushr and similar dues even on permitted income. In this way Islam has closed the doors of the social ills found in the present-day capitalistic system. And if monopolies are nonetheless created at any time, the government has been permitted to intervene and break them up.

**On economic equality.** From *"and We raised some of them above others in ranks"* Maʿārif argues that economic equality — in the sense that everyone's income should be equal — is neither desirable nor practically feasible. Allah has charged every member of this universe with some duties and given rights in proportion to those obligations. And among human beings likewise, those whose duties exceed others' have been given more rights: the prophets (peace be upon them), whose responsibilities exceed those of all other human beings, were given more in many respects.

Allah has applied the same principle to the economic system: economic rights are given in accordance with duties and obligations. Since equality in duties is not possible — abilities differ in physical strength, health, intellectual power, age, level of intelligence, efficiency and quickness, and no state however advanced can make people homogeneous in these — differences in economic duties are unavoidable, and therefore differences in income are unavoidable too; for if everybody's income were made equal while duties remained different, equity and justice could not be established. Determining such differences precisely is an extremely sensitive and difficult task for which man has no perfect standard — which is why, Maʿārif says, it has been kept in the domain of nature. Where a state takes control of all means of production, that impossible measurement falls to a few government functionaries: such discretionary powers give rise to corruption and nepotism — and even supposing all those functionaries were angels sincerely desiring justice, by what measure would they determine the difference between the duties of an engineer and a labourer?

**What Islamic equality does mean.** The equality Islam has established is in the matters of law, social behaviour, and the honouring of everyone's rights: everybody is equal in exercising his legal, civil and social rights to obtain his economic dues. What it does not mean is that a rich man or a man of rank should obtain his right with ease and dignity while a poor man has to knock on doors and lose his self-respect to obtain his — or that the law should protect the rights of the rich and leave the poor to fend for themselves. This kind of inequality is not tolerable in Islam, and this, Maʿārif notes, is what Sayyidunā Abū Bakr aṣ-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) said in one of his addresses: **"I swear by Allah that nobody is more forceful to me than a weak man until I cause his right to be given to him, and nobody is weaker than a powerful man till I obtain from him the right of the weak one."** Economically, Islamic equality means that everybody should have equal opportunity to earn a livelihood; Islam does not tolerate a few wealthy persons controlling and monopolising the sources of wealth while small traders are unable to do business in the market place. An environment of freedom is created in which every individual can earn according to his ability, endeavour and investment.

**The closing clause of ayah 32 puts that whole ledger in its place:** *"But the mercy of your Lord is better than what they amass."* Ibn Kathir: the mercy of Allah towards His creation is better for them than the wealth and conveniences of this world which they possess.

## The silver houses: ayat 33–35

**Ayah 33** begins: *"And were it not that mankind would have become of one community…"* Ibn Kathir gives the meaning, which he attributes to Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others: were it not for the fact that many ignorant people would think that Allah's giving them wealth was a sign that He loves the one to whom He gives it — and would thus have agreed upon disbelief for the sake of wealth.
