If that danger did not exist, Allah says, He would have provided for those who disbelieve in ar-Raḥmān — the Most Gracious — silver roofs for their houses, and elevators, meaning (as Ibn Kathir explains, with Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, as-Suddī, Ibn Zayd and others) ladders and staircases of silver by which they would go up; **ayah 34** adds doors — Ibn Kathir notes, locks on their doors — and thrones on which they could recline, all of that made of silver; and **ayah 35** caps it with *adornments*, which Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, as-Suddī and Ibn Zayd explained as **gold**.

The picture is deliberately excessive, and it is offered *to those who reject Him*. Ibn Kathir titles this section plainly: wealth is not a sign of divine pleasure. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it just as plainly: wealth and property are so worthless in Allah's view that, if there were no apprehension of people becoming disbelievers, He would have showered gold and silver upon all the infidels. Neither abundance of wealth can be a cause of someone's superiority, nor can poverty be taken as an indication of his being lower in rank.

Maʿārif adds a merciful qualification: the statement that all the people would have become disbelievers is meant of *most* people. Even today there are people who are certain that if they abandoned faith they would gain abundant wealth, and they do not lose their faith for it; such people would perhaps have remained steadfast even then — but their number would have been very little indeed.

**Then the verdict:** *"Yet all this would have been nothing but an enjoyment of this world."* Ibn Kathir: all that belongs to this transient world, which is insignificant before Allah. He hastens the reward of good deeds in the form of luxuries in this world, so that when such a person reaches the Hereafter he will have no good merits with Allah for which he may be rewarded — as was reported, Ibn Kathir says, in the authentic hadith.

Ibn Kathir then cites a narration on the worthlessness of this world: **"If this world were worth a gnat's wing before Allah, He would not give a disbeliever a drink of water,"** noting that al-Baghawī narrated its chain of narration. He reports it again, in slightly fuller wording — **"He would never give a disbeliever a drink of water"** — as reported by at-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah, via Abū Ḥāzim from Sahl bin Saʿd, with at-Tirmidhī's grading: "Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ."

**The last clause of ayah 35 is the door out of all of it:** *"And the Hereafter with your Lord is for those who have taqwā"* — *taqwā* being the consciousness by which a person keeps his duty to Allah. Ibn Kathir: it is *exclusively* for them, and no one else will share it with them. Silver ceilings can be handed to anyone. The Hereafter cannot.

## From the Sunnah, and how to live it

Ibn Kathir sets down a scene that turns this passage from argument into life. ʿUmar bin al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) visited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in seclusion, when he was keeping away from his wives, and saw him resting on a rough mat which had left marks on his side. ʿUmar's eyes filled with tears and he said: "O Messenger of Allah, look at this Chosroes and this Caesar with all that they have, and you are the best of Allah's creation." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had been reclining; he sat up and said, **"Are you in doubt, O son of al-Khaṭṭāb?"** Then he ﷺ said, **"Those are people for whom the enjoyments are hastened in this world."** According to another report: **"Does it not please you that this world is for them and the Hereafter is for us?"**

Ibn Kathir then cites, from the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and elsewhere, the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: **"Do not drink from vessels of gold and silver, and do not eat from plates of the same, for these things are for them in this world and for us in the Hereafter."** The silver of ayah 33 and the gold of ayah 35 are their portion now; the believer declines them here and receives them there.

- **Stop reading wealth as a verdict.** Neither abundance of wealth is a cause of superiority, nor is poverty a sign of being lower in rank, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states directly. It cuts both ways: do not look down on the poor believer, do not envy the prosperous unbeliever.
- **Accept that you are not the distributor.** Not of prophethood, not of provision. Ayah 32 places both firmly in Allah's hands. That is a rebuke to arrogance and, for the one who accepts it, a release from anxiety.
- **Take the difference in ranks as a design for interdependence, not a licence for exploitation.** Ayah 32 states the purpose: that some may employ others in their work, because one needs the other and the other needs him. Where big capitalists take undue advantage and compel the poor to work for less than their entitlement, Maʿārif's remedies stand — the injunctions of ḥalāl and ḥarām, a wide-ranging code of ethics based on the concept of the Day of Retribution, and the authority of an Islamic government to set wages in such abnormal conditions.
- **Weigh the world at its true weight.** In Ibn Kathir's phrase, it is insignificant before Allah. Then work in it honestly, spend from it, and set your heart on what ayah 35 reserves exclusively for the people of taqwā.

passages.title: The devil companion of the heedless
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat trace one life from beginning to end. A person deliberately looks away from Allah's Reminder; a devil is assigned to keep him company; that companion steers him off the road while he congratulates himself on his direction; and on the Day of Resurrection the two of them stand together, the man wishing the width of the world lay between them — only to be told that the wish is useless and the punishment is shared. What holds ayat 36–39 together is that single thread: **the companion you get is the consequence of the Reminder you refused.**

## Ayah 36 — "Turns a blind eye": the word ya'shu

Everything begins with the verb. Ibn Kathir explains that *al-ʿAshā*, the root behind *yaʿshu*, refers to **weakness of vision** — and that what is meant here is **weakness of insight**. So the Qur'an does not say "whoever disbelieves" or "whoever denies"; it says, in effect, *whoever goes dim-sighted toward the Reminder of the Most Compassionate*.

That image matters, because dimming your own sight is not a violent act. It is a quiet one. Ibn Kathir glosses it as "whoever **willfully** ignores and turns away," and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is just as pointed: "whoever **knowingly** turns a blind eye towards Allah's advice i.e. the Holy Qur'an and *waḥy* (revelation)." The blindness described here is not an affliction someone suffers; it is a posture someone adopts. The light is there. The eyes are simply half-shut, and kept that way.

Notice also **what** is turned away from and **Who** it belongs to: *dhikr ar-Raḥmān*, the Reminder of the Most Compassionate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies this Reminder as the Qur'an and revelation itself. And the divine name chosen is the one of overflowing mercy — Ibn Kathir titles this whole section "The Shaytan is the Companion of the One Who turns away from **Ar-Raḥmān**." The thing being brushed aside is not a demand from a distant power; it is guidance from the Most Compassionate.

## Ayah 36 — "We appoint for him a devil"

*Nuqayyiḍ lahu shayṭānan fa-huwa lahu qarīn* — "We appoint for him Shaytan to be a Qarin (a companion) to him."

This is the sentence that unsettles people, so read it in the order the ayah gives it. **The turning away comes first; the assignment comes second.** Ibn Kathir establishes this by placing three other ayat alongside it:

- *"And whoever contradicts and opposes the Messenger after the right path has been shown clearly to him"* (4:115) — after clarity, not before it.
- *"So when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away"* (61:5) — their turning preceded, His decree followed.
- *"And We have assigned for them intimate companions, who have made fair seeming to them, what was before them and what was behind them"* (41:25) — the same verb of assigning, the same result of a beautified illusion.

So this is not an arbitrary sabotage of an innocent person. It is what Ibn Kathir describes plainly: "for this person who **willfully neglects** true guidance, We send to him a Shaytan to lead him astray and show him the path to Hell." The appointing is Allah's — the ayah says *We appoint* — and what the ayah teaches is that the sentence fits the crime with terrible precision: refuse the best company available to a human being, and you are handed the worst.

The word *qarīn*, which Ibn Kathir renders simply as "a companion," means an intimate — the one who is always there. Not an enemy across a battlefield, but a presence at your shoulder.

## The companion who never takes a day off

Here Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up something easy to miss. Citing Qurṭubī, it explains that this assigned devil "accompanies him **all the time** in this world to prevent him from virtuous deeds, and to divert him towards evil. When such a man is resurrected in the Hereafter, his devil will also be with him, till they both are pushed in Hell."

Two jobs, then: **preventing good and diverting towards evil.** And no expiry date — this attachment runs from the turning-away in this world all the way to the Fire.

Then a further precision, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes to Bayān ul-Qurʼān: this assigned devil is **in addition to** the shayṭān attached to every human being, believer and disbeliever alike. The difference is in the pattern of presence. That ordinary shayṭān "does leave the man alone at certain specific times, whereas **this devil accompanies him all the time**." Every person faces this attachment; that is the human condition. What ayah 36 describes is a heavier state — an unbroken escort, given to the one who made the refusal a settled habit.

**And there is a punishment here that lands long before the Fire.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, again on Qurṭubī's authority, draws it out: "the punishment one gets **even in this world** for turning away from Allah's remembrance is that he gets into bad company." Note that the devils spoken of here are "whether from humans or from jinns" — the corrupting companion may be an unseen whisperer or may be the friend sitting beside you, and the effect is the one Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names: being steadily "diverting him from virtues to vices." If you have ever wondered how a person's circle silently reshaped his life, this ayah is describing the mechanism, and calling it a punishment already in progress.

## Ayah 37 — Hindered, and delighted with themselves

*"And verily, they hinder them from the path, but they think that they are guided aright."*

Two things happen in this ayah, and the second is worse than the first.

The first is obstruction: the companions "hinder them from the path." That is what a devil-companion does — not necessarily by arguing you out of religion, but by standing between you and the road.

The second is the sting in the tail: **"but they think that they are guided aright."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the state exactly: "He commits vices but thinks that he is doing very well." Compare 41:25, which Ibn Kathir cites here: the assigned companions "made fair seeming to them, what was before them and what was behind them." The work of such a companion is cosmetic. He does not tell you that wrong is right; he makes wrong *look* right, until self-satisfaction closes the last exit.

This is the most frightening line in the passage, because it removes the ordinary alarm system. A man who knows he is astray may repent tomorrow. A man convinced he is guided has no reason to.

## Ayah 38 — The wish that arrives too late

*"Till, when (such a one) comes to Us, he says: Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts — a worst companion (indeed)!"*

The eyes open at last, and open at the worst possible moment. Ibn Kathir: "When he comes before Allah on the Day of Resurrection, he will **complain about the Shaytan** who was appointed to accompany him."

The measure of distance he reaches for is *buʿd al-mashriqayn*, which Ibn Kathir renders "the distance of the two easts (or the east and west)." Either way it is the maximum span a person can picture: the whole width of the horizon, one end of the world to the other. That is how far he now wants his old inseparable friend. The one whose company he never questioned in life is now described in a single scalding phrase — *fa-bi'sa al-qarīn*, **"a worst companion (indeed)!"**

Ibn Kathir also records a variation in how the opening of the ayah was read: "Some of them recited it *ḥattā idhā jā'ānā*" — "Till, when **they both** come to Us" — "referring to the companion Shaytan and the one whom he accompanies." Read that way, the picture sharpens: they arrive **together**, still paired, still inseparable, standing before Allah — and it is precisely then that one of them begs to be rid of the other.

There is a bitter honesty in that timing. Nothing new is revealed to him on that Day; the Reminder had told him this from the start. All that has changed is that the dim sight of ayah 36 has finally been forced wide open.

## Ayah 39 — "It will profit you not this Day"

*"Since you were wrongdoers, it will never benefit you today that you are sharing the punishment with each other."*

The reply comes, and it closes every door at once. Ibn Kathir: "your being together in the Fire will not help you in the slightest, and you will both partake of the painful punishment."

Two things deserve attention. First, the address is **plural** — spoken to both parties, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering makes plain, and as Ibn Kathir's "you will **both** partake" confirms. The man does not get to stand as a victim who was merely led astray while his companion takes the blame; each of them carries what he earned. Second, the clause *idh ẓalamtum*, "since you did wrong" — the reason the wish is refused is not cruelty but a wrong already established.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers **two explanations** of this ayah, and both are worth carrying away:

**One:** since your *kufr* (disbelief) and *shirk* (ascribing partners to Allah) has been proved, your longing in the Hereafter — "Will that this devil had been away from me" — will be of no avail, because all of you will be sharing the same punishment. The wish is refused because the verdict is already established.

**Two:** the sharing itself will bring you no relief. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes with real psychological insight that in this world, "indeed it happens that when a few people share the same misfortune, everyone's burden of misery becomes somewhat lighter" — trouble held in common is trouble halved. "But there in Hell, everybody will be so terrorized that nobody will be able to lighten another's misery and hence sharing of the punishment will be of no benefit." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that its own rendering of the ayah is built on this second reading.)

That is the last consolation being removed. Shared misfortune is one of the mercies of this life — even the shared groan of fellow sufferers eases something. On that Day, terror is so total that no one has anything left over to give anyone else. The companionship that felt so warm on earth turns out to have been an arrangement with no comfort in it at all, and the two who could not be separated in life will find that being together buys them nothing.

## Living it

The passage does not moralise; it simply lays out a chain, and every link is a place to act.

**Guard the Reminder — and notice the half-shut eye.** The chain begins not with a great sin but with a slow drift: the Qur'an unopened, the reminder heard and shrugged off, the sight allowed to go dim. Ibn Kathir's gloss — *weakness of insight* — names something most of us can recognise in ourselves before it hardens.

**Take your company seriously.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls bad company a punishment received *even in this world*, and it explicitly includes devils "from humans" alongside those from the jinn. The friend who reliably makes the wrong choice look reasonable is doing precisely what ayah 37 describes.

**Fear the comfortable conscience most.** *"They think that they are guided aright."* A settled feeling that all is well is not evidence that all is well. The corrective is the very thing ayah 36 says was abandoned — coming back to the Reminder of the Most Compassionate and letting it, not your own contentment, tell you where you stand.

**Do not save the regret for the Day it cannot help.** The man of ayah 38 eventually says exactly the right thing about his companion. Ayah 39 answers that the right words at the wrong time buy nothing. Everything he wished for then — distance from that companion — was fully available to him earlier, at the cost of simply looking up when the Reminder came.

Read together, ayat 36–39 are a mercy in the shape of a warning. Allah is showing a person the end of the road while he still has the power to leave it — and the Reminder he is being called back to is, in the ayah's own words, the Reminder of *ar-Raḥmān*, the Most Compassionate, the very One the heedless man was turning away from.

passages.title: You cannot make the deaf hear — hold fast to the revelation
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat turn away from the disbelievers and speak to the Prophet ﷺ himself. Allah has just described a man who willfully turns away from the remembrance of Ar-Rahman, for whom a Shaytan is appointed as a *qarin* — a constant companion — and who on the Day of Resurrection will stand before Allah complaining about that very companion (43:36–39). Now He addresses His Messenger ﷺ directly, and the whole passage moves as one act of consolation: first He lifts from the Prophet ﷺ a burden that was never his (ayah 40), then He guarantees that justice will reach his enemies whether or not he lives to see it (41–42), and then He tells him what *is* his to do — hold fast to the revelation (43), know what that revelation is worth (44), and know that every messenger before him carried the very same message (45).

## Why the question is asked at all (ayah 40)

To feel ayah 40 you have to hear what comes immediately before it. Ibn Kathir walks through it: *"And whosoever Ya'shu (turns away blindly) from the remembrance of the Most Gracious, We appoint for him Shaytan to be a Qarin (a companion) to him."* The verb is **yaʿshu**, and Ibn Kathir explains that its root, **al-ʿAsha**, refers to weakness of vision — but here what is meant is weakness of *insight*. This is not a man who cannot see; it is a man who will not look. He "willfully ignores and turns away," in Ibn Kathir's words. And the consequence is terrifying in its exactness: the man lets his own sight go dim, and a devil is appointed to accompany him.

Ibn Kathir places this alongside three other ayat that describe the same divine pattern — *"And whoever contradicts and opposes the Messenger after the right path has been shown clearly to him"* (4:115), *"So when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away"* (61:5), and *"And We have assigned for them intimate companions, who have made fair seeming to them, what was before them and what was behind them"* (41:25). The order matters in all three: the turning away comes first, the abandonment second. Ibn Kathir's own gloss makes the mechanism plain: for the person who willfully neglects true guidance, "We send to him a Shaytan to lead him astray and show him the path to Hell." And Allah says of these companions that "they hinder them from the path, but they think that they are guided aright" — the cruellest detail in the scene. The man is being steered toward Hell while feeling entirely certain he is right.

Then comes the reckoning. He cries out, *"Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts – a worst companion (indeed)!"* Ibn Kathir notes that some recited the phrase before it as **ḥattā idhā jāʾānā** — "Till, when they both come to Us" — referring, he says, to the companion Shaytan and the one whom he accompanies, arriving together. And Allah's answer: *"It will profit you not this Day as you did wrong, (and) that you will be sharers in the punishment."* Ibn Kathir's gloss is blunt — your being together in the Fire will not help you in the slightest, and you will both partake of the painful punishment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers two readings of that line. One: since your *kufr* and *shirk* — disbelief and ascribing partners to Allah — have been proved, your longing in the Hereafter to be rid of this devil will be of no avail, because all of you will be sharing the same punishment. The other: in this world it does happen that when a few people share the same misfortune, everyone's burden of misery becomes somewhat lighter. But in Hell everybody will be so terrorized that nobody will be able to lighten another's misery, so sharing the punishment will be of no benefit at all. Company in the Fire is not company.

**And it is out of that scene that ayah 40 comes.** *"Can you make the deaf to hear, or can you guide the blind or him who is in manifest error?"* Ibn Kathir's answer is immediate: *"that is not up to you."* The deafness and blindness here are not of the ears and eyes; they are the condition just described — insight gone dim by the man's own choice. You cannot pour hearing into ears that have shut themselves.

Ibn Kathir then draws the line the Prophet ﷺ needed to see: *"All you have to do is convey the Message, but you do not have to guide them. Allah guides whomsoever He wills and sends astray whomsoever He wills, and He is Wise and Just in doing so."*

Hold both halves of that. Allah's will is absolute — guidance is His to give and withhold, not the Messenger's to manufacture. And, as Ibn Kathir immediately adds, He is Wise and Just in doing so. Ibn Kathir affirms both together without collapsing either: the will belongs to Allah alone, and it is exercised with perfect wisdom and justice. For the Prophet ﷺ, who wanted his people saved, this is release. The result was never on his shoulders. Only the delivery was.

## Vengeance is certain — the only question is the timing (ayat 41–42)

Ayat 41 and 42 are two branches of a single promise. *"And even if We take you away, We shall indeed take vengeance on them"* — Ibn Kathir: *"We will inevitably wreak vengeance upon them and punish them, even if you pass away."* The Prophet's ﷺ death would not cancel the reckoning; it would only mean he did not witness it.

*"Or (if) We show you that wherewith We threaten them, then verily, We have perfect command over them"* — and Ibn Kathir glosses this simply: *"We are able to do both."* Whether the Messenger ﷺ is present or absent, Allah's command over them is complete.

But Ibn Kathir does not leave the two branches evenly balanced. He continues that Allah will not take His Messenger ﷺ in death until He gives him the joy of seeing his enemies brought low and gives him power and authority over them and their wealth. This, he says, was the view of **As-Suddi**, and it was the opinion favoured by **Ibn Jarir**. So the ayah states the possibility in both directions, and this reported view leans it toward mercy for the Prophet ﷺ.

There is a quiet lesson in the framing itself. Allah did not tell His Messenger ﷺ *when*. He told him *that*. Certainty about the outcome, patience about the schedule — that is the posture the passage is teaching.

## "So hold fast" (ayah 43)

**Fa-stamsik bi-lladhī ūḥiya ilayk** — *"So hold you fast to that which is revealed to you."* Notice where the command falls: right after the promise of vengeance. The instruction is not "wait for them to be punished" but "take hold of what has been given to you."

Ibn Kathir explains: hold fast to the Qur'an which has been sent down *to your heart*, for it is truth and what it leads to is truth — truth that shows the way to the straight path, and that path leads to the Gardens of Delight and to eternal, everlasting goodness.

Read that chain carefully, because it answers a real worry. The Book is true. What it leads to is true. It shows the way to the straight path. The straight path leads to the Gardens of Delight and to goodness without end. There is no weak link anywhere in it. And then the reassurance in the second half of the ayah: *"Verily, you are on the straight path."* When almost everyone around you is refusing, the doubt that creeps in is not usually "is the message true?" but "am I doing this right?" Allah settles it before it can take root.

## The Qur'an as your honour — and your examination (ayah 44)

*"And verily, this is indeed a **Dhikr** for you and your people, and you will be questioned."*

Ibn Kathir gives two reported readings of **dhikr** here.

**First: honour.** He reports that it means "it is an honor for you and your people," and names those who held it — **Ibn ʿAbbas** (may Allah be pleased with him), **Mujahid**, **Qatadah**, **As-Suddi** and **Ibn Zayd**. Then he explains *why* it is an honour, and the reason is sobering rather than flattering: it is an honour for them in that it was revealed in their language, so they are the people who have the best understanding of it among mankind — and hence are obliged to be the most steadfast in adhering to its commandments. Ibn Kathir adds that this is precisely how the best of them were: the first immigrants, and those who emulated them and followed them. Privilege of access is converted directly into weight of responsibility.

**Second: reminder.** He also reports the reading that it means "it was sent to remind you and your people." And he adds a crucial guard against a narrow reading: the fact that they are singled out does not exclude others. He cites *"Indeed, We have sent down for you (O mankind) a Book in which there is Dhikrukum (your Reminder). Will you not then understand?"* (21:10) and *"And warn your tribe of near kindred"* (26:214). Being named first is a starting point of the address, not a fence around it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up the "honour" sense and says that *dhikr* here means 'good name' or 'fame' — the Qur'an is a matter of great honour and good fame for the Prophet ﷺ and his people. It reports that **Imam Razi** concluded from this ayah that good fame is a desirable thing, because Allah has stated it here as a matter of favour; and that this is why Sayyidnā Ibrahim (peace be upon him) supplicated, *"And destine for me a truthful description among the next generations"* (26:84).

But Maʿārif immediately fences that off, and the fence is essential: good fame is praiseworthy only when it is received as an automatic result of virtuous deeds. When virtuous deeds are done *for the sake of* good fame, it becomes **riyāʾ** — ostentation — which not only nullifies all the rewards of good deeds but also renders one guilty of a major sin. Reputation is a gift to be received, never a target to be aimed at.

On "**your people**," Maʿārif notes that some exegetes took the phrase to mean the tribe of Quraysh only, thereby proving a superiority of Quraysh — but reports that **ʿAllamah Qurtubi** says that according to the correct view these words refer to the whole Ummah of the Prophet ﷺ, irrespective of colour or race, and that the Qur'an is a matter of honour and good fame for the whole Ummah. That is the reading that carries down to us: the honour of this Book belongs to every believer who holds it, not to a bloodline.

**"And you will be questioned."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and lands hard: you will be questioned *about this Qur'an* — how you acted upon it and what your response to it was. In a single ayah the Book is named as your greatest distinction and as the subject of your examination. The same thing that raises you is the thing you will be asked about.

## Ask the messengers who came before (ayah 45)

The passage closes by widening from one Prophet ﷺ to all of them: *"And ask whom We sent before you of Our Messengers: 'Did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Gracious?'"*

Ibn Kathir's meaning: all the Messengers called their people to the same as that to which you are calling mankind — namely the worship of Allah alone with no partner or associate — and they forbade the worship of idols and false gods. He cites *"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah (nation) a Messenger (proclaiming): 'Worship Allah, and avoid all false deities.'"* (16:36). The Prophet ﷺ was not bringing a novelty that Makkah could dismiss as invention. He was restoring the single message of every prophet who had ever come.

Ibn Kathir also records a variant transmission: **Mujahid** said that **ʿAbdullah bin Masʿud** (may Allah be pleased with him) recited it as *"And ask those whom We sent before you of Our Messengers"* — narrated from Ibn Masʿud by **Qatadah**, **Ad-Dahhak** and **As-Suddi**. But Ibn Kathir is careful, and his caution is a model of scholarly honesty: this appears to be an *explanation* rather than an alternate version of recitation. And Allah knows best.

**How can the Prophet ﷺ "ask" prophets who had already died?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises this question directly, since all the earlier prophets (peace be upon them) had passed away by the time this ayah was revealed. Some exegetes took the ayah to mean that if Allah were to arrange such a meeting as a miracle, he should ask them — and Maʿārif notes that it is well established that the Prophet ﷺ met all the preceding prophets (peace be upon them) during the Night of Ascension. Maʿārif adds that ʿAllamah Qurtubi quotes some narrations according to which the Prophet ﷺ asked them this very thing after leading them in prayer — but Maʿārif states, with commendable frankness, that it could not discover the source of these narrations. Take it as reported, not as established.

Most exegetes, Maʿārif says, therefore explained that the ayah does not mean asking the prophets verbally at all. What is meant is to **consult the divine Scriptures revealed to the earlier prophets, and to ask their learned scholars**. And Maʿārif makes the striking point that the scriptures of the prophets of the Children of Israel that are available now — despite so many distortions — still contain teachings about *tawhid* (the Oneness of Allah) and condemnation of *shirk* (associating others with Allah) even today. It quotes, as examples, Deuteronomy 4:35 and 6:4, declaring that the Lord alone is the true deity and that there is no other, and calling Israel to love the Lord with all the heart; Isaiah 45:5–6, where the Lord declares there is no other god and that this will be known from one end of the world to the other; and the words attributed to Sayyidnā Masīḥ (peace be upon him) in Mark 12:29 and Matthew 22:36, calling Israel to hear that the Lord alone is their Lord, and to love Him with all the heart, soul, mind and strength. It also cites the supplication attributed to him in John (Yuhanna) 17:3, that eternal life means knowing the only true deity. Maʿārif notes that these excerpts are taken from the Good News Bible, Today's English Version, published by the Bible Societies in 1976.

The argument is beautifully direct: you do not need to summon a prophet from the grave. Open what is left of what they brought, and the answer is still legible. Tawhid is not Muhammad's ﷺ innovation. It is the one message.

## Living it

**Deliver, and let go of the result.** Ibn Kathir's line on ayah 40 is the whole ethic of daʿwah: your duty is to convey; guidance belongs to Allah. When a parent, a sibling, or a friend will not hear, ayah 40 is not permission to stop caring — it is release from a burden that was never yours. Even the Prophet ﷺ was told, of making the deaf hear, "that is not up to you."

**Guard your own insight before you worry about anyone else's.** The deafness in ayah 40 began as **yaʿshu** in ayah 36 — the willful ignoring and turning away from the remembrance of Ar-Rahman that leaves the insight weak, until the person believes he is guided aright while he is being led away. Ibn Kathir's chain is a warning about small, chosen turnings-away.

**Watch who walks beside you.** The passage's picture of the *qarin* — a companion who makes wrong things look fair, whom you will one day wish were the distance of the two easts away — is worth applying to the company, the voices and the feeds that keep you company now.

**Grip the Book.** *"So hold you fast to that which is revealed to you"* is not a suggestion to admire the Qur'an. It is the instruction given to the Prophet ﷺ at the moment of maximum opposition, and Ibn Kathir's chain says the grip ends in the Gardens of Delight.

**Let the honour be a summons.** Ibn Kathir's reasoning in ayah 44 is that the honour of the Qur'an is precisely the reason to be most steadfast in adhering to its commandments, and Maʿārif's warning is that fame sought for its own sake becomes riyāʾ. Both point the same way: the distinction is real, and it is not yours to display — it is yours to answer for. *"And you will be questioned."*

passages.title: Moses sent to Pharaoh with signs
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat compress the confrontation between Musa (peace be upon him) and Pharaoh into a single arc: a messenger sent with signs, a court that laughs, signs that grow greater until they become punishment, a desperate plea for relief, and — the moment relief arrives — a broken promise. The thread holding the passage together is not the miracles themselves but what a hardened heart does with them.

## Why this story is being told here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point that unlocks the whole passage. The events of Musa's mission are told repeatedly in the Qur'an, and these particular incidents have been described in detail in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf. So why recall them here, in this compressed form?

Because of the objection the disbelievers of Makkah were making about the Prophet ﷺ — that he was not a wealthy man, and therefore, in their reckoning, not the sort of person to be given prophethood. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that this objection is not new at all. Pharaoh had expressed the same doubt against Musa (peace be upon him) and his prophethood. His contention was that, being the ruler of Egypt and owner of the palaces and the rivers flowing beneath them, how could Musa claim to be a prophet against him?

And then the answer, which is really a warning: just as Pharaoh's disbelief could be of no avail to him — he drowned along with his people — so this objection of the disbelievers of Makkah will not save them from the divine punishment, in this world or in the Hereafter.

So when you read these five ayat, hear them as they first landed: the objection is old, the pattern is known, and the ending has already been written once before.

## Ayah 46 — sent to Pharaoh *and his chiefs*

"And indeed We did send Musa with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs."

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that here Allah tells us about His servant and Messenger Musa, peace be upon him, and how He sent him to Pharaoh and his chiefs.

And note that the mission is not aimed at Pharaoh alone. The *malaʾ* — his chiefs — are, in Ibn Kathir's explanation, his governors, his ministers, his leaders, and their followers, among both the Egyptians and the Children of Israel. Tyranny is never one man. It is a whole apparatus of officials and courtiers, and the call reached all of them.

What was Musa sent to say? Ibn Kathir states it plainly: Allah sent him to call them to worship Allah alone, with no partner or associate, and to forbid them from worshipping anything other than Him. That is the core of the mission — *tawḥīd*, the oneness of Allah in worship. Not political reform first, not liberation first: the summons to worship the One.

And the words the ayah gives Musa are worth pausing over: **"Verily, I am a Messenger of the Lord of all that exists."** He says this standing before the ruler of Egypt, the owner of its palaces and the rivers beneath them. Musa announces a Lordship so much larger that Pharaoh's holdings shrink to nothing beside it.

**The signs he brought.** Ibn Kathir lists them: mighty signs such as his hand and his staff, and other signs such as the flood, the locusts, the *Qummal*, the frogs and blood, and the loss of their crops and their lives.

## Ayah 47 — the laughter

"But when he came to them with Our signs, behold, they laughed at them."

Ibn Kathir's summary is stark: despite all of that, they remained arrogant and stubbornly refused to follow him; they rejected his message and made fun of it, and laughed at the one who had brought it.

This is worth sitting with, because laughter is a specific kind of rejection. An argument can be answered. A question can be examined. But ridicule refuses to engage at all; it dismisses the matter as beneath serious attention and makes the one who brought it look foolish. And the one dismissed this way was Musa, peace be upon him, carrying signs from the Lord of all that exists.

## Ayah 48 — each sign greater than the one before

"And not a sign We showed them but it was greater than its fellow preceding it, and We seized them with torment, in order that they might turn."

The Arabic reads *illā hiya akbar min ukhtihā* — literally, "except that it was greater than **its sister**." The signs are spoken of as a family, one after another, each one greater than the one before it.

Ibn Kathir's comment on their response is devastating in its plainness: despite that, they would not give up their sin, their misguidance, their ignorance and their confusion.

**And now the most merciful phrase in the passage.** Allah says He seized them with torment "in order that they might turn." The punishment itself was not the objective. It was aimed at their return. Even the flood and the locusts and the frogs were, in their own harsh way, a summons: *come back*. This is how the ayah teaches us to read hardship that lands on the disobedient — as a door still being held open, not merely a sentence being carried out.

## Ayah 49 — "O sorcerer!"

"And they said: 'O you sorcerer! Invoke your Lord for us according to what He has made a pact with you. Verily, we shall guide ourselves.'"

Modern ears hear *yā ayyuhā al-sāḥir* as an insult, and it is easy to read this as Egyptians spitting the word "magician" at a Prophet even while begging him for help. Ibn Kathir records a different and far more interesting reading, which he attributes to **Ibn Jarir**: here *sāḥir* means the expert, the knowledgeable one.

Ibn Kathir explains the reasoning carefully. The scholars of that time were the sorcerers or magicians, and magic was not regarded by them at that time as something reprehensible — so this was not a slight on their part. More telling still is the situation itself: they were in a state of need, so it would not have been appropriate for them to insult him. This was, as Ibn Kathir puts it, a way of honouring him, as they thought.

Which is, in its own way, more damning than an insult would have been. At the height of their need they reached for a title of respect: master of knowledge. They could see he had something real. They still would not call him what he actually was — a Messenger of the Lord of all that exists.

**"According to what He has made a pact with you."** They appeal to the covenant between Musa and his Lord — the standing relationship they know he has, the fact that when he asks, he is answered. They are, in effect, borrowing a believer's access to Allah without becoming believers themselves.

**"Verily, we shall guide ourselves."** This is the promise. Ibn Kathir describes what it meant in practice: on each occasion, they promised Musa that if the torment were lifted from them, they would believe in him and let the Children of Israel go with him.

## Ayah 50 — the moment the pressure lifts

"But when We removed the torment from them, behold, they broke their covenant."

Ibn Kathir completes the sentence: but on each occasion they went back on their word. Not once — *on each occasion*. Ibn Kathir notes that every time one of these signs came to them, they would go and implore Musa. So this was a cycle, run again and again: sign, plea, promise, relief, betrayal.

Ibn Kathir places alongside this the parallel passage in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf, which spells the same cycle out at length:

> "So We sent on them: the flood, the locusts, the *Qummal*, the frogs, and the blood; manifest signs, yet they remained arrogant, and they were of those people who were criminals. And when the punishment struck them, they said: 'O Musa! Invoke your Lord for us because of His promise to you. If you remove the punishment from us, we indeed shall believe in you, and we shall let the Children of Israel go with you.' But when We removed the punishment from them **to a fixed term, which they had to reach**, behold! they broke their word!" (7:133–135)

That phrase carries the sting: the relief they received was not a pardon. It was a removal of punishment only until a fixed term they were going to reach anyway.

## Living it

**Signs do not create faith on their own; they meet a heart already inclined one way or the other.** Pharaoh's court saw the staff and the hand, saw the flood, saw the locusts — and laughed, then bargained, then broke their word. Ibn Kathir's own summary is that despite all of it they would not give up their sin, their misguidance, their ignorance and their confusion. The obstacle was never a shortage of evidence.

**Watch the shape of a foxhole promise.** Everyone knows the vow made in the hospital corridor, in the turbulence, in the week the money runs out: *if You take this away from me, I will change.* Ayah 50 is a mirror held up to that vow. The test of the promise is not the sincerity you feel while making it — they promised on each occasion, and each time the need was real. The test is what you do the morning the pressure lifts. A believer's practical safeguard is to turn the panic-prayer into something concrete and immediate while the fear is still fresh, rather than trusting a resolution that has never yet survived contact with relief.

**Read hardship as an invitation.** Ayah 48 tells us the seizing was so that they might turn. When difficulty comes, the first question a believer asks is not "why me" but "what is this calling me back to?"

**And take the comfort the passage was sent to give.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is that the sneer of the powerful — *you have no wealth, so who are you?* — is one of the oldest objections there is, and it has never once been an argument. Pharaoh had the palaces and the rivers flowing beneath them. His disbelief was of no avail to him; he drowned along with his people.

passages.title: Pharaoh's boast and his people's ruin
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat give us a scene: Pharaoh gathers his people, makes a speech, wins them over — and then, in two short ayat, the whole civilisation he was boasting about is under water. What holds the passage together is a single argument about how people judge truth. Pharaoh's case against Musa (peace be upon him) is built entirely on appearances: I have a kingdom, he has nothing; I speak well, he stammers; where are his gold bracelets and his escort of angels? The passage lets him make that case at length (ayat 51–53), records that it worked (ayah 54), and then answers it not with a counter-argument but with the sea (ayat 55–56).

## Why this story, here

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the connection that unlocks the passage. Incidents from the life of Musa (peace be upon him) are told repeatedly in the Qur'an, and these particular events have already been described in detail in Sūrah al-Aʿrāf. So why recall them again here?

Because, Maʿārif explains, the objection of the disbelievers of Makkah — that the Prophet ﷺ was not a wealthy man — is not a new objection at all. Pharaoh had expressed the same doubt against Musa (peace be upon him) and his prophethood: his contention was that, being the ruler of Egypt and the owner of the palaces and the rivers flowing beneath them, how could Musa (peace be upon him) claim to be a prophet against *him*?

And Maʿārif draws the conclusion the passage is driving at: just as Pharaoh's disbelief could be of no avail to him, and he was drowned along with his people, this objection of the disbelievers of Makkah will not save them from the divine punishment either — not in this world, nor in the Hereafter.

The old story is being held up beside the present objection, and the two are shown to be the same objection.

## Ayah 51 — the boast

Ibn Kathir opens by telling us what kind of moment this is: Allah tells us how Pharaoh stubbornly persisted in his rebellion and disbelief. He assembled his people and addressed them in a vainglorious fashion, boasting of his dominion over Egypt.

**"Is not mine the dominion of Egypt, and these rivers flowing underneath me?"** Qatadah's comment fills in the picture: "They had gardens and rivers of flowing water." Pharaoh is not gesturing at an abstraction. He is pointing at the visible, green, watered abundance of the land he governs and calling it his.

**"See you not then?"** Ibn Kathir explains: he means *do you not see my position of might and power?* — implying that Musa (peace be upon him) and his followers were poor and weak. The argument is never stated outright, because it does not need to be. It is the oldest and laziest argument there is: look at me, and look at him.

Ibn Kathir sets this speech alongside another passage about the same man: *"Then he gathered (his people) and cried aloud, saying: 'I am your lord, most high.' So Allah seized him with punishment for his last and first transgression"* (79:23–25). The same pattern — gather the crowd, raise the voice, claim the height — and the same ending.

## Ayah 52 — "this one who is despicable"

Two insults, both examined closely by the commentators.

**مَهِين (mahīn).** As-Suddi said that Pharaoh's question is really a statement: he was saying, "indeed I am better than this one, who is despicable." Some of the grammarians of Basrah likewise said that Pharaoh was claiming he was better than Musa (peace be upon him). Ibn Kathir's answer is blunt: this is an obvious lie, may continued curses be upon him until the Day of Resurrection.

What did Pharaoh mean by the word? The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites each catch a different shade of it:
- **Sufyan:** insignificant.
- **Qatadah and As-Suddi:** weak.
- **Ibn Jarir:** he had no power, authority or wealth.

What the three glosses have in common is worth noticing. Not one of them is a moral charge. Insignificance, weakness, no power or wealth — the whole indictment is that Musa (peace be upon him) counts for nothing in the world's ledger.

And Ibn Kathir turns the word straight back on the man who used it: Pharaoh's description of Musa (peace be upon him) as "despicable" is a lie; rather it is *he* who was despicable and insignificant, lacking in physical, moral and religious terms, and it is Musa (peace be upon him) who was noble, truthful, righteous and upright.

**وَلَا يَكَادُ يُبِينُ — "and can scarcely express himself clearly."** Ibn Kathir gives the surface sense: he cannot speak clearly, he stammers and cannot speak well. And then he says plainly: this too was a lie. Something had happened to Musa's tongue when he was a child, when it was burnt by a coal. He asked Allah to loosen the knot from his tongue — to correct the speech defect — so that his people could understand what he said, and Allah answered his prayer: *"You are granted your request, O Musa"* (20:36).

Ibn Kathir then mentions the possibility Al-Hasan Al-Basri suggested: it may be that some problem remained which Musa (peace be upon him) had not asked to be relieved of, since he had asked only to be relieved of what stood in the way of conveying the Message. And Ibn Kathir states the principle that follows: **a person cannot be blamed for physical matters over which he has no control.** He adds that Pharaoh had the intelligence to understand that perfectly well — he simply wanted to confuse and mislead his people, who were ignorant.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds two readings of the taunt, citing Tafsīr Kabīr and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī:
1. The stammering had already been removed by Allah in answer to Musa's own supplication, but Pharaoh remembered only his previous state — hence the aspersion.
2. Or Pharaoh did not mean stammering in speech at all, but meant that Musa (peace be upon him) could not put forward arguments adequate to satisfy him. This, says Maʿārif, was nothing but a false accusation, because Musa (peace be upon him) had completely overwhelmed Pharaoh with his arguments and proofs, against which Pharaoh had no answer.

Either way the mechanism is the same: the man who has lost the argument attacks the voice.

## Ayah 53 — bracelets and angels

**"Why then are not golden bracelets bestowed on him?"** Ibn Kathir explains: adornments which are placed on the arms — the view of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him), Qatadah and others.

**"Or angels sent along with him?"** — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, angels to serve him and to testify that he is telling the truth. Pharaoh wants an entourage: visible, impressive, and on display.

Then Ibn Kathir gives the verdict on the whole speech in one line: **he looked only at outward appearances and did not understand the true inner matters that are clearer than what he focused on — if only he had understood that.** Pharaoh was not short of evidence. He was short of willingness to look at it.

## Ayah 54 — how a nation is talked into ruin

**فَٱسۡتَخَفَّ قَوۡمَهُۥ فَأَطَاعُوهُ** — Ibn Kathir: he confused them and invited them to misguidance, and they responded to him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, that the Arabic sentence can be rendered in two ways:
1. **"He made a fool of his people"** — the reading its translation adopts.
2. **"He easily made his people follow him."**

The two readings sit together well: he treated them as weightless, and steering them cost him nothing.

But the ayah does not leave the crowd as mere victims. **"Verily, they were ever a people who were rebellious."** Their obedience to him is placed alongside a description of what they already were.

## Ayah 55 — "when they angered Us"

**فَلَمَّآ ءَاسَفُونَا** — Ibn Kathir gathers the early explanations. ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥa reported that Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said it means: they provoked Our wrath. Ad-Daḥḥāk said it means: they made Us angry. Ibn Kathir notes this was also the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, Muḥammad bin Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, Qatadah, As-Suddi and other scholars of tafsīr.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, adds a caution about how the phrase is to be understood: since Allah Almighty is pure of the states of anger and sorrow, the meaning is that their behaviour caused Him to decide that they should be punished.

What is beyond dispute is the timing. The kingdom, the rivers, the obedient crowd — all of it was still in Pharaoh's hands while he was making that speech. The punishment comes in the next sentence of the sūrah, not in that one.

**A warning from the Sunnah.** Ibn Abī Ḥātim recorded that ʿUqbah bin ʿĀmir (may Allah be pleased with him) said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"When you see that Allah gives a person what he wants even though he is persisting in sin, that means that Allah is enticing him into destruction."* Then he recited this very ayah — *"So when they angered Us, We punished them, and drowned them all."*

The word the hadith uses for that enticement is **istidrāj**. Blessings arriving on top of disobedience are not by themselves a verdict of approval.

Two further reports Ibn Kathir attaches to this ayah:
- It was reported that Ṭāriq bin Shihāb said: "I was with ʿAbdullāh (may Allah be pleased with him), and the issue of sudden death was mentioned. He said, 'It is a relief for the believer and a source of regret for the disbeliever.'" Then he recited this ayah.
- ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAzīz (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I found that punishment comes with negligence" — meaning, again, this ayah. Heedlessness is not a harmless state; it is the state in which the seizure arrives.

**"And drowned them all."** The king who claimed the rivers, and the crowd who obeyed him, went into the same water.

## Ayah 56 — made into a lesson

**فَجَعَلۡنَٰهُمۡ سَلَفٗا وَمَثَلٗا لِّلۡأٓخِرِينَ** — "And We made them a precedent, and an example to later generations."

Two words, two functions, explained by the early authorities Ibn Kathir cites:

- **سَلَفًا — a precedent.** Abū Mijlaz said: "Precedent for others who do the same as they did." Their end now stands as the standing notice attached to that road.
- **مَثَلًا — an example.** Abū Mijlaz and Mujāhid said: "An example, i.e., a lesson to those who come after them." Their ruin became a permanent teaching for those who came later.

There is a quiet irony in this ending. Pharaoh spent his speech asking to be *looked at* — "See you not then?" He got his wish. Generations have looked at him ever since, and seen the opposite of what he wanted them to see.

## Living it

**Stop reading power as proof.** Pharaoh's whole case was that visible might settles the question of truth. Ibn Kathir's line is the one to keep: he looked only at outward appearances and did not understand the true inner matters that are clearer than what he focused on.

**Do not judge a person by what they cannot help.** Musa (peace be upon him) was mocked for what had happened to his tongue in childhood. Ibn Kathir states the principle without qualification — a person cannot be blamed for physical matters over which he has no control. Mockery of someone's speech, body or poverty is Pharaoh's argument, whoever makes it.

**Weigh what you are being told.** The crowd in ayah 54 did not lose their religion in a battle. They lost it in a speech: he confused them and invited them to misguidance, and they responded to him — and the ayah adds that they were ever a people who were rebellious.

**Read your own comfort carefully.** Ease alongside persistent sin may be istidrāj, as the hadith recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim warns. The right response to blessing is gratitude and repentance, not the assumption that things must be going well.

**And take the passage as it was given.** Ayah 56 says outright that Allah made them a precedent and an example for those who came after — which means you. Ibn Kathir closes the passage with the only sound conclusion: Allah is the One Who guides to the straight path, and unto Him is the final return.

passages.title: Jesus raised as a taunt: only a servant
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat capture a scene from the streets of Makkah: the Quraysh think they have caught the Prophet ﷺ in a contradiction, they burst out at their own cleverness, and Allah answers them — first by exposing the motive behind the objection, then by stating in a few Arabic words exactly what 'Isa ibn Maryam (peace be upon him) really was. What holds the passage together is a single question: **who and what is the son of Maryam?** Ayah 57 shows the uproar, ayah 58 the taunt and its exposure, ayah 59 the answer, ayah 60 the removal of the misunderstanding that made the taunt possible in the first place.

## The argument that caused the uproar

Ibn Kathir gives the background from Muhammad ibn Ishaq in *As-Sirah*. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sat down one day with al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah in the Masjid when an-Nadr ibn al-Harith came and sat down with them, and other men of Quraysh were in the gathering. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ spoke; an-Nadr came up to him, and the Prophet ﷺ spoke with him until he ﷺ defeated him in argument. Then he ﷺ recited to him and to them:

> "Certainly you and that which you are worshipping now besides Allah, are (but) fuel for Hell! (Surely) you will enter it." (21:98)

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ got up and went to sit with 'Abdullah ibn az-Zab'ari at-Tamimi. Al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah said to him: "By Allah, an-Nadr ibn al-Harith could not match the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib in argument. Muhammad claims that we and these gods that we worship are fuel for Hell." Ibn az-Zab'ari answered, "By Allah, if I meet with him I will defeat him in argument," and produced what he thought was the winning move: *ask Muhammad whether everyone that is worshipped instead of Allah will be in Hell with those who worshipped him — for we worship the angels, and the Jews worship 'Uzayr, and the Christians worship the Messiah 'Isa ibn Maryam.*

Al-Walid and those sitting with him were amazed at what Ibn az-Zab'ari said, and they thought that he had come up with a good point. Ibn Ishaq's report continues that this was put to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: *"Everyone who likes to worship something other than Allah will be with the one whom he worshipped, for indeed they are worshipping the Shaytan and whomever told them to worship that person."* (This wording comes from Ibn Ishaq's *Sirah* as Ibn Kathir relays it; the bundle names no hadith collection for it.) Allah then revealed, "Verily, those for whom the good has preceded from Us, they will be removed far therefrom" (21:101) — which, Ibn Kathir explains, means 'Isa, 'Uzayr, and rabbis and monks who were also worshipped, who had spent their lives in devotion towards Allah; it was the misguided people who came *after* them who took them as lords instead of Allah. Concerning the notion of worshipping angels as daughters of Allah came the words, "Glory to Him! They are but honored servants" (21:26). And concerning 'Isa ibn Maryam being worshipped instead of Allah — and the amazement of al-Walid and the others present at that argument — came our ayah 57.

Ibn Kathir also records, from Ibn Jarir reporting al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), a compressed version of the same exchange: when 21:98 was said to the Quraysh they asked, "What about 'Isa ibn Maryam?" The Prophet ﷺ replied, **"He is the servant and Messenger of Allah."** They then said, "By Allah, he means that we should take him as a lord just as the Christians took 'Isa son of Maryam as a lord." And Allah answered them with ayah 58: *they quoted not the above example except for argument.*

## Three reported occasions, one answer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the exegetes report **three** events as the background of these ayat:

1. The Prophet ﷺ addressed the Quraysh and said, "O people of Quraysh, there is no good in whatever is worshipped beside Allah," and the polytheists responded that the Christians worship 'Isa (peace be upon him) — although you yourself say that he was a virtuous slave of Allah and His prophet (reported from Qurtubi).
2. The objection raised by 'Abdullah ibn az-Zab'ari against 21:98, as above — at which the polytheists of Quraysh became very joyful (reported from Ibn Kathir and others).
3. The pagans of Makkah expressed the absurd thought that the Prophet ﷺ wanted to claim godhead for himself, so that he might be worshipped the way the Christians worship 'Isa.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then makes an important point: **in reality there is no conflict between the three.** The disbelievers will have said all three things, and Allah revealed these ayat in a manner comprehensive enough to take care of all three objections at once. As for the third, the answer is quite clear in the passage itself: those who began worshipping 'Isa did so in obedience to no divine command, 'Isa never desired it for himself, and the Qur'an gives it no support — so how is it then possible that the Prophet ﷺ would claim godhead in imitation of the Christians?

## Ayah 57: what "yaṣiddūn" describes

The Arabic says that when the son of Maryam was *ḍuriba mathalan* — quoted, held up, as an example in argument — "at once your people **yaṣiddūn** from it." The early authorities describe that reaction from slightly different angles, and the differences are worth feeling:

- **Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, as-Suddi and ad-Dahhak** (may Allah be pleased with them) said: *they laughed* — that is, they were astounded by that.
- **Qatadah** said: they were *repelled* by that and they laughed.
- **Ibrahim an-Nakha'i** said: *they turned away.*

Put together, you get the whole picture of a crowd that hears something it cannot refute honestly: the noisy laugh, the recoil, the turning of the back.

Ibn Kathir sums up the meaning of the ayah plainly: they take this argument as a basis for rejecting your message.

## Ayah 58: the taunt, and the word that unmasks it

"And they said: *Are our gods better, or is he?*" Qatadah explained what they were driving at: they were saying, *our gods are better than him.* Qatadah also transmitted that Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) recited the words as **"a-ālihatunā khayrun am hādhā"** — "are our gods better, or **this one**?" — and on that recitation the "this one" they were sneering at is Muhammad ﷺ himself.

Then comes the verdict: **"mā ḍarabūhu laka illā jadalan"** — "they quoted not the above example except for argument." *Jadal* is disputation for the sake of disputation: contention pursued to win, not to arrive at truth. Ibn Kathir explains why this is the exact diagnosis: it means for the sake of stubborn argument, **because they knew that 'Isa was not included in 21:98**, since that would not make sense. That ayah was addressed to the Quraysh, for they used to worship idols and false gods. They did not worship the Messiah — so why should he be included in what the ayah says? What they said was only for the sake of argument; they did not really believe in it.

That is the sting of the passage. This was never an intellectual difficulty. It was a debating move, and Allah exposes it as one. The closing words seal it: **"bal hum qawmun khaṣimūn"** — nay, but they are a quarrelsome people. Not a people with a question, but a people with a habit.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Umamah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"No people go astray after having been guided, but they resort to (futile) argument."* Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this very ayah: "They quoted not the above example except for argument. Nay! But they are a quarrelsome people." Ibn Kathir adds that it was also recorded by at-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir, and that at-Tirmidhi said, "This hadith is Hasan Sahih, we do not know it except from the hadith of Hajjaj bin Dinar..." — that is, at-Tirmidhi graded it *hasan sahih* while noting that he knew it only through that one line of transmission.

This is a warning aimed at us as much as at Quraysh. Argumentativeness is presented here not as a sign of sharp thinking but as a **symptom of having lost the way** — what a people fall into once guidance has slipped from their hands. It is worth asking honestly, before entering any religious dispute: am I trying to find the truth, or trying to win?

## Ayah 59: "He was not more than a servant"

After all the noise, Allah's answer about 'Isa (peace be upon him) is stunningly short: **"in huwa illā 'abdun an'amnā 'alayh"** — the Arabic *in ... illā* is a construction of pure restriction: *he is nothing whatsoever except* a servant upon whom We bestowed favour.

Ibn Kathir: this means 'Isa, peace be upon him — he was no more than **one of the servants of Allah** whom Allah blessed with prophethood and messengership.

Notice how the ayah both lowers and raises him in the same breath. It lowers the claim: *'abd*, a servant — the same word the Prophet ﷺ used of him when Quraysh asked, "He is the servant and Messenger of Allah." And it raises the man: *an'amnā 'alayh*, **We** granted Our favour to **him** — prophethood and messengership are not achievements he seized but gifts Allah placed upon him. Servanthood is not the opposite of honour here. It is the container of it.

"**And We made him a mathal for the Children of Israel.**" Ibn Kathir explains: a sign, proof and evidence of Our power to do whatever We will. This is a reversal of the taunt. Quraysh had "struck" 'Isa as a *mathal* — an argumentative example — against the Prophet ﷺ. Allah replies that He had already made him a *mathal*, but of a different kind altogether: not ammunition in a dispute, but a demonstration of divine power set before Bani Isra'il.

## Ayah 60: dismantling the misunderstanding at its root

"And if it were Our will, We would have made angels to replace you on the earth." The commentators explain the picture in complementary ways:

- **As-Suddi**: they would have taken your place on the earth.
- **Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah** (may Allah be pleased with them): they would have succeeded one another just as you succeed one another. Ibn Kathir notes that this view is implied by the former.
- **Mujahid**: they would have populated the earth instead of you.

Why does this come here, immediately after 'Isa is called a servant? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the connection, and it is the key that unlocks ayah 60. This is **a reply to the gravely mistaken conclusion the Christians drew from the miraculous birth of 'Isa (peace be upon him) without a father** — from which they attributed godhead to him and began to worship him. Allah answers, to controvert their argument, that this birth was **merely a demonstration of His power**. He has power to do even more extraordinary things: He created Adam (peace be upon him) without father and mother. And if He wills, He may do things as unprecedented as causing angels to be born out of human beings.

Follow the logic and the misunderstanding collapses. An unusual origin proves the power of the One who caused it, not the divinity of the one who came from it. And the Lord who could, if He wished, have angels succeed you on this earth is manifestly not a Lord who needs a son.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a further point that clears 'Isa (peace be upon him) entirely. The statement that all objects of worship besides Allah will become fuel for Hell — and the Prophet's ﷺ statement that there is no good in whatever is worshipped besides Allah — refers to **lifeless objects of worship such as idols, and to those living beings who directed their followers towards their own worship or who liked to be worshipped**, such as the shayatin, Fir'awn and Namrud. 'Isa is obviously not included in that category, since at no stage did he like to be worshipped. The Christians did not worship him because of any direction given by him; rather they were misled, deducing the wrong conclusion from his birth without a father — a birth that was itself a sample of Allah's power, showing people that Allah does not need even any apparent cause or means in order to create. Their worship of him was not only irrational, it was **against his own teachings**, because he had always preached *tawhid*, the Oneness of Allah. His own disgust at being worshipped simply does not allow his inclusion in the ranks of false gods.

Ibn Kathir's commentary runs straight on from here into the next ayah, where 'Isa is described as a sign for the Hour — but that lies beyond the four ayat before us and belongs to the passage that follows.

## Living it

**Truth is not decided by who wins the room.** Ibn az-Zab'ari's objection impressed the gathering; al-Walid and those sitting with him thought he had come up with a good point. Their approval settled nothing. Allah exposed the objection as *jadal* while the amazement was still fresh.

**Beware of arguing to win.** The hadith of Abu Umamah ties argumentativeness directly to a people losing guidance they once had. When you catch yourself hunting for a clever counter rather than for what is true, that is the very disease this passage names.

**Honour a righteous servant without crossing the line into worship.** The tragedy Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes is not that the Christians thought highly of 'Isa (peace be upon him) — Allah Himself says "We granted Our favor to him" — but that reverence drifted into a worship he never asked for and always preached against. The safe place is exactly where the Prophet ﷺ put him: **the servant and Messenger of Allah.** Any love for a prophet or a righteous person that ends anywhere other than the worship of Allah alone has gone wrong.

**Read miracles correctly.** A wonder points to the One with power over it. That is what ayah 60 teaches: the fatherless birth was a display of Allah's power, and that same power could, if He willed, put angels on this earth in our place.

passages.title: Jesus, sign of the Hour, calls to worship
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat close the Qur'an's answer to a debating trick the Quraysh were proud of. Having just said that 'Isa (Jesus), peace be upon him, was nothing more than a servant whom Allah favoured (ayah 59), Allah now says what he really is: a sign that the Hour is coming — and then lets 'Isa himself speak, so that the man the Quraysh were arguing about turns out to be preaching the very message they were rejecting. The thread holding ayat 61–65 together is one line, said twice: **"This is the straight path."** Allah says it in ayah 61, 'Isa says it in ayah 64, and both times it means the same thing — worship Allah alone.

## The argument these ayat are answering

Briefly, the setting. Ibn Kathir gives the background from Muhammad bin Ishaq's *As-Sirah*. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ had defeated An-Nadr bin Al-Harith in argument in the Masjid and recited to him and to the gathering: *"Certainly you and that which you are worshipping now besides Allah, are (but) fuel for Hell!"* (21:98). Afterwards 'Abdullah bin Az-Zab'ari proposed a counter-argument: ask Muhammad whether everyone who is worshipped instead of Allah will be in Hell with those who worshipped him — for we worship the angels, the Jews worship 'Uzayr, and the Christians worship the Messiah 'Isa bin Maryam. Al-Walid and those sitting with him were amazed at this and thought he had come up with a good point.

The Prophet ﷺ answered — in the wording of that same narration — *"Everyone who likes to worship something other than Allah will be with the one whom he worshipped, for indeed they are worshipping the Shaytan and whomever told them to worship that person."* And Allah revealed: *"Verily, those for whom the good has preceded from Us, they will be removed far therefrom"* (21:101) — which, Ibn Kathir explains, covers 'Isa, 'Uzayr, and the rabbis and monks who were also worshipped, who had spent their lives in devotion towards Allah and were then taken as lords by misguided people who came after them.

Ibn Kathir is blunt about why the objection was dishonest: they knew perfectly well that 'Isa was not included in 21:98, because that would not make sense. That ayah is addressed to the Quraysh, who worshipped idols and false gods. They did not worship the Messiah — so why should he be included in what the ayah says? What they said was only for the sake of argument; they did not really believe in it. Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Umamah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"No people go astray after having been guided, but they resort to (futile) argument"* — and then he ﷺ recited the ayah about the Quraysh's quarrelling. Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir, and that At-Tirmidhi said the hadith is Hasan Sahih. It is a sobering diagnosis: clever argument is often not the cause of misguidance but its symptom.

That is the argument. Ayah 61 is the answer.

## Ayah 61: "And he shall be a known sign for the Hour"

**وَإِنَّهُۥ لَعِلۡمٞ لِّلسَّاعَةِ**

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* lays out two explanations of this phrase:

1. That 'Isa's being born without a father is proof that Allah can create people without apparent causes — so resurrecting the dead is not at all difficult for Him. On this reading, his very existence is an argument for the resurrection.
2. That his descent from the sky is a sign of the Day of Judgement. *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* says most exegetes have taken the ayah in this second sense, and that his coming to this world again in its last days and his killing of the Dajjal (the Antichrist) is proved by *mutawātir* ahadith — narrations carried by so many independent chains that they cannot reasonably be doubted. (It refers the reader to the author's own longer works on the subject for more detail.)

Ibn Kathir holds the second to be the correct view: the phrase refers to 'Isa's descent before the Day of Resurrection. He supports it with *"And there is none of the People of the Scripture but must believe in him before his death"* (4:159) — where "his death" means the death of 'Isa, peace be upon him — followed by *"and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them."* He adds that this meaning has support from an alternate recitation of the ayah, *wa innahu la-'alamun lis-sā'ah*, which means evidence that the Hour will surely come. Mujahid said the ayah means a sign, and that "one of the signs of the Hour will be the appearance of 'Isa son of Maryam before the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Kathir reports something similar from Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Al-'Aliyah, Abu Malik, 'Ikrimah, Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and others, and adds that many *mutawātir* hadiths report that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said 'Isa will descend before the Day of Resurrection **as a just ruler and fair judge**.

Ibn Kathir also passes on a third angle worth holding alongside these: the miracles and signs that happened at his hands, such as raising the dead and healing the sick, are sufficient as signs of the approach of the Hour. The dead rising at his hands is already a foretaste of the day when all the dead will rise.

Notice how completely this dismantles the Quraysh's objection. They had used 'Isa to score a debating point about who ends up in the Fire. Allah answers that 'Isa is not a problem for the message — he is *evidence for it*, and specifically evidence for the very Hour these people were denying.

**فَلَا تَمۡتَرُنَّ بِهَا — "Therefore have no doubt concerning it."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and absolute: do not doubt that it will surely come to pass. This is not a suggestion to be less sceptical; it is a command to stop entertaining the doubt at all.

**وَٱتَّبِعُونِ — "And follow Me."** Ibn Kathir explains: *in what I tell you about it*. The Hour is not something anyone can investigate for himself; the only access to it is revelation. Believing in it and following what has been revealed about it are one and the same act.

**هَٰذَا صِرَٰطٞ مُّسۡتَقِيمٞ — "This is the straight path."** Ibn Kathir explains the phrase where it recurs in ayah 64: the straight path is the worship of the Lord, may He be exalted, alone.

## Ayah 62: the enemy who works on the road

**وَلَا يَصُدَّنَّكُمُ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنُ** — "And let not Shaytan hinder you." Ibn Kathir supplies the missing word: hinder you **from following the truth**. First the doubt, then the distraction — the two prohibitions come one after the other.

*"Verily, he to you is a plain enemy."* There is nothing hidden about the enmity; what is hidden is only the method. And the narration behind this passage has already shown the method at work: the Quraysh thought they were making a brilliant argument about angels and 'Uzayr and the Messiah, while the Prophet ﷺ had already identified what people in that position are really doing — *"they are worshipping the Shaytan and whomever told them to worship that person."*

## Ayat 63–64: 'Isa speaks for himself

Having been argued *about* for several ayat, 'Isa is now allowed to speak. It is a devastating turn: the Quraysh's supposed trump card opens his mouth and preaches the worship of Allah alone.

**"And when 'Isa came with clear proofs" (بِٱلۡبَيِّنَٰتِ)** — the evidences that authenticated him.

**"I have come to you with Al-Ḥikmah"** — Ibn Kathir: meaning **prophethood**. Wisdom here is not general good sense; it is the office and what came with it.

**"and in order to make clear to you some of that in which you differ."** Ibn Jarir said this means *religious* matters, not worldly ones — and Ibn Kathir comments, "What he said is good." *Maʿārif ul Qurʼān*, citing *Bayan-ul-Qur'an*, fills in the history: since Bani Isra'il were drowned in arrogance and obstinacy, they had tampered with the Divine laws, and 'Isa disclosed the reality of such distortions. The word **"some"** is precise: some other matters they differed over were purely of a mundane nature, and he might not have felt the need to deal with those. This is a quiet lesson about what revelation is for. It came to correct religion, not to arbitrate every human disagreement.

**"Therefore have Taqwa of Allah, and obey me."** Ibn Kathir reads the two commands as a pair with two different objects: have taqwā of Allah *with regard to what I command you to do*, and obey me *in what I bring to you*. Taqwā — mindfulness of Allah, the awareness that makes a person careful — is owed to Allah; obedience is owed to the messenger precisely because what he brings is from Allah. There is no rivalry between the two.

**"Verily, Allah! He is my Lord and your Lord. So worship Him."** This is the heart of the passage, and it is 'Isa himself who says it. Ibn Kathir draws out the force of *my Lord and your Lord*: "you and I are enslaved to Him, in need of Him, and we commonly share in the worship of Him alone, associating none with Him." The one whom later generations would worship stands on the same side of the line as everyone else — a servant, needy, worshipping. Then: *"This is the straight path"* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, that what he has brought to them is the straight path, which is the worship of the Lord, may He be exalted, alone. The phrase Allah used in ayah 61 is repeated by 'Isa in ayah 64, sealing the two halves of the passage into one message.

## Ayah 65: and then they split

**"But the sects from among themselves differed."** Ibn Kathir: they differed and became parties and factions. Some stated that he was the servant and Messenger of Allah — *which is true*. Others claimed that he was the son of Allah, or that he himself was Allah — glorified be Allah far above what they say.

Read the sequence and the tragedy lands: in ayah 63 he came precisely *to make clear to them some of what they differed over*; in ayah 65 they differed about **him**. The one thing he had told them plainly — Allah is my Lord and your Lord — became the one thing they disagreed about.

**"So woe to those who do wrong from the torment of a painful Day."** Note the wording: not a painful torment, but the torment of a painful *Day*. The day itself is described as painful, so that everything in it is coloured by that pain. This is the same Hour that ayah 61 told the Quraysh not to doubt. The passage ends where it began.

## Living it

**Recognise argument for argument's sake — first of all in yourself.** The Quraysh's objection was clever and completely insincere; Ibn Kathir says plainly that they did not really believe what they were saying. The Prophet's ﷺ words recorded by Imam Ahmad make the warning personal: a people given guidance and then given to quarrelling are a people already slipping.

**Let the certainty of the Hour actually change something.** "Have no doubt concerning it" is a command, not a mood. The passage attaches it directly to "follow Me" — the practical proof that a person believes the Hour is coming is that he follows what has been revealed about it.

**Guard the line 'Isa drew.** *My Lord and your Lord.* Ibn Kathir's phrase — that we are enslaved to Allah and in need of Him — is the cure for every form of excess about righteous people. Honouring the prophets and the pious is part of faith; giving them anything of worship is the wrongdoing that ayah 65 leaves under a "woe."
