**Expect the enemy at the moment of clarity.** Ayah 62 comes immediately after the truth is stated plainly, not before. The hindering happens on the straight path, not off it — which means the pull to delay, to argue, to be distracted is often strongest just when the way forward has become clear.

passages.title: The Hour, and the mindful in Paradise
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** After the surah has recalled ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) and his mission — sent, as ayah 63 says, "to explain to you some of those matters in which you differ" — the discourse turns from argument to the moment when all argument ends. Ayat 66–73 take us from the Hour crashing in on people who were not watching for it (66), through the collapse of every worldly friendship into hatred (67), to a call that singles out one group alone and ushers them into a Garden described in warm, sensory detail (68–73).

What holds the eight ayat together is a single question running quietly underneath them: **who will you be standing next to on that Day, and will they still be on your side?** The Hour arrives without warning; relationships are sorted; the people of taqwā are addressed by Allah Himself, reassured, named, and told to enter. Everything from ayah 68 onward is speech directed *to* the believers — the passage becomes a welcome.

## Ayah 66 — the Hour arrives while they are looking the other way

Ibn Kathir reads the opening as a rebuke aimed at "these idolaters who disbelieve in the Messengers." The form of the question — *are they waiting for anything except the Hour?* — implies that this is, in effect, all they are doing: waiting, without knowing it, for the one event they refuse to prepare for.

Two Arabic words carry the weight: **بَغْتَةً (baghtatan) — "suddenly," by surprise** — and **وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ — "while they perceive not,"** while they have no sense of it coming. Ibn Kathir joins these to a point of creed: the Hour "is real and will inevitably come to pass, and these negligent people are unprepared for it." The Hour is not uncertain; only its timing is hidden. The uncertainty is on our side, not in the event.

He then names the outcome with terrible precision: "When it comes, it will catch them unawares, and on that Day they will feel the utmost regret when regret will not benefit them in the slightest and will not afford them any protection." Regret is knowledge arriving too late. The passage does not say the heedless will never understand — it says they will understand perfectly, at the one moment when understanding buys nothing.

## Ayah 67 — the day friendships change sides

**"Close friends will be enemies to one another on that Day, except the muttaqīn."** Ibn Kathir states the principle plainly: "every friendship that exists for a purpose other than for the sake of Allah will turn to enmity on the Day of Resurrection, except for that which is for the sake of Allah, which will last forever."

Notice how much this ayah claims. It does not say that bad friendships end. It says they *invert*. Affection does not simply evaporate; it becomes hostility, because each friend now sees the other as the one who helped bring him here.

Ibn Kathir supports this with the words of Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) to his people in Sūrat al-ʿAnkabūt: *"You have taken idols instead of Allah. The love between you is only in the life of this world, but on the Day of Resurrection, you shall disown each other, and curse each other, and your abode will be the Fire, and you shall have no helper"* (29:25). Shared falsehood does create real warmth in this life — Ibrāhīm concedes the *mawaddah*, the mutual love. He only points out its expiry date.

**The one exception: taqwā.** The exception is not "except close friends" but "except *the muttaqīn*" — those who have taqwā, a mindful and watchful care about how one lives before Allah. What survives the Day is not the intensity of a friendship but its foundation.

### ʿAlī's discourse on the two pairs of friends

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws this ayah out at length, calling it a verse that "tells us plainly that the friendly relations in which we take so much pride in this world, and for which we don't even care about halal and Haram, will be of no use on the Day of judgment, rather they will turn into enmity."

It then relays a discourse of Sayyidnā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), which — as Maʿārif reports — Ibn Kathir reproduced, narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzāq in his *Musannaf* and by Ibn Abī Hātim. (This is the speech of a Companion, not a report from the Prophet ﷺ.) It describes two pairs of friends.

**The believing pair.** One of them dies first. When he is given the glad tidings of Paradise, his first thought is not of himself but of the friend he left behind, and he prays: "O Allah! That friend of mine used to advise me to obey You and to obey the Holy Prophet ﷺ, he used to direct me towards virtues and to prevent me from vices, and kept on reminding me that one day I would have to meet You. So O Allah! Do not misguide him after me, so that he may also see the scenes of Paradise as You have shown to me, and be pleased with him, as You have been with me." He is answered: "Do not worry, if you know what reward I have stored for your friend, you will weep less and laugh more." Later the second dies too, their souls are brought together, and each is directed to praise the other — and each says of his companion that he was the best brother, the best companion and the best friend.

**The disbelieving pair.** The pattern is identical, and inverted at every point. Told he is bound for the Fire, the first remembers his friend and prays: "O Allah! That friend of mine used to insist upon me to disobey You and Your messenger, used to direct me towards vices and used to prevent me from virtues and used to tell me that I would never meet You. So O Allah! Do not give him guidance after me, so that he may also see the scenes of Hell, as You have shown to me, and be displeased with him just as You have been displeased with me." And when the two souls are brought together and directed to praise each other, each says: he was the worst brother, the worst companion and the worst friend.

Read the two prayers side by side and the ayah becomes almost unbearably clear. Both men pray for their friend — one that he be guided, one that he *not* be. Each prayer is the natural extension of what the friendship already was. The Day of Judgement does not manufacture the enmity of ayah 67; it makes visible what a friendship was doing all along.

### What "friendship for the sake of Allah" means

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes that "the best friendship, in respect of this world as well as the Hereafter, is the one that is for the sake of Allah," and notes that many merits are stated in hadith for two Muslims who love one another purely for Allah's sake — among them that they will be in the shade of the ʿArsh, the Throne of Allah. (The source does not name a collection for those reports, so we pass on the teaching without attaching it to one.)

It also defines the term, which saves it from vagueness: **love for the sake of Allah "means to love someone because he is a true follower of the religion prescribed by Allah."** Maʿārif adds that this includes sincere love for teachers of religious subjects, spiritual guides, reformers, religious scholars and devotees of Allah — and for all the Muslims.

**Living it.** The test the passage suggests is not "do I like this person?" but "what is this friendship *for*?" A friendship built around what Allah loves — one that pushes you toward good, restrains you from wrong, and keeps reminding you that you will meet Him — is being built for permanence. Maʿārif's sharpest line concerns the friendships for which "we don't even care about halal and Haram": when keeping a friend costs you obedience to Allah, the ayah has already told you where that friendship ends.

## Ayat 68–69 — the call, and the qualifier

**"O My servants! There is no fear for you this Day, nor shall you grieve"** (68) — then, immediately, **"those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims"** (69). Ibn Kathir explains ayah 69 as meaning that "their hearts believed and they submitted inwardly and outwardly to the Laws of Allah" — inward faith and outward submission together, neither standing in for the other.

Ibn Kathir preserves a striking illustration of why these two ayat come in this order, from al-Muʿtamir bin Sulaymān, who narrated it from his father:

> "When the Day of Resurrection comes and the people are resurrected, there will be no one left who will not be filled with terror. Then a caller will cry out: *'My servants! No fear shall be on you this Day, nor shall you grieve.'* So all the people will be filled with hope, but this will be followed by the words: *'(You) who believed in Our Ayat and were Muslims.'* Then all of mankind will be filled with despair apart from the believers."

Feel the sequence. Universal terror; a call of pure reassurance that lifts every heart in the gathering; then one clause that narrows the address to a single group — and hope drains out of everyone else. For one instant, everyone thinks the call is for them.

Note the address itself — *yā ʿibādi*, **"O My servants."** The believers are not merely acquitted; they are spoken to by their Lord as His own, and told that both directions of human anxiety are closed off: no *fear* for what is coming, no *grief* for what is past.

## Ayah 70 — "Enter Paradise, you and your spouses, rejoicing"

Ibn Kathir's glosses here are short and precise:

- **ادْخُلُوا الْجَنَّةَ** — "Enter Paradise" means, in his words, "they will be told to enter Paradise." It is a command, and being commanded into the Garden is itself the honour.
- **أَنْتُمْ وَأَزْوَاجُكُمْ** — "you and your *azwāj*", which Ibn Kathir explains as "your counterparts." The believers do not enter alone.
- **تُحْبَرُونَ (tuḥbarūn)** — Ibn Kathir renders this as being "in delight and joy."

## Ayah 71 — the Garden through the senses

**"Golden trays and cups will be passed around to them."** Ibn Kathir describes the *ṣiḥāf* and *akwāb* as "fine vessels of gold containing food and drink, without spouts or handles."

**"There will be whatever the souls desire and the eyes delight in."** Ibn Kathir mentions that some recited the phrase as **مَا تَشْتَهِيهِ الْأَنْفُسُ** rather than **مَا تَشْتَهِي الْأَنْفُسُ**; he glosses both the same way — whatever the souls desire. As for "all that eyes could delight in," he explains it as "good food, delightful fragrances and beautiful scenes."

That gloss is worth pausing on. Ibn Kathir's explanation of what "the eyes delight in" names good food and fragrance alongside beautiful scenes — taste and scent as well as sight. And the phrase the ayah itself uses is not a list of items but a measure: *whatever the souls desire*.

**"And you will abide therein forever."** Ibn Kathir's comment on *khālidūn* adds something the word alone does not: "you will never leave it or want to exchange it." Two things are secured — permanence, and contentment with the permanence. No one there will grow restless in it.

## Ayah 72 — inherited by deeds, entered by mercy

**"That is the Paradise which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."** Ibn Kathir says this is spoken to them "as a reminder of the blessing and favor of Allah," and then draws the balance this ayah exists to teach:

> the righteous deeds "were the cause of your being included in the mercy of Allah. For no one will be admitted to Paradise by virtue of their deeds alone; that will be by the mercy and grace of Allah. But the varying ranks and degrees of Paradise will be attained according to one's righteous deeds."

This holds together two truths that are easily pulled apart. Deeds are not the purchase price of Paradise — entry is by Allah's mercy and grace. Yet deeds are not idle either: in Ibn Kathir's words they are the *cause* by which one comes to be included in that mercy, and they decide the differing ranks within the Garden.

## Ayah 73 — the last touch

**"There you will have abundant fruit to eat from."** Ibn Kathir: "fruits in plenty" means "of all kinds," and "of which you will eat" means "whatever you choose and desire."

Then he makes an observation about the Qur'an's manner of description: "When food and drink are mentioned, fruit is also mentioned to complete the picture of blessing and joy." The fruit comes after the food and drink — the touch that completes the picture. A passage that began with the Hour falling on the unprepared closes on the smallest and most gracious of details — and Ibn Kathir ends his own comment where a scholar should: *"And Allah knows best."*

## Holding the passage together

Set the two halves against each other and the design shows. In ayah 66 people are taken by surprise by something they had been told was coming. In ayah 67 they discover their closest companions are now against them. From ayah 68 the believers experience the opposite at every point: no fear and no grief; not alone, but with their counterparts; trays and cups passed round to them; and not passing through, but abiding forever — never leaving it, in Ibn Kathir's phrase, and never wanting to exchange it.

And the hinge between the two halves is a single quality — **taqwā** — which shows itself in something as ordinary as the company a person keeps. Ayah 67 sorts the whole of humanity by the answer to one question: were your loves for Allah's sake, or for something that dies when the world does?

passages.title: The wicked in the unrelenting torment
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat give us the state of the people of the Fire: the sentence passed on them (74–75), the justice of that sentence (76), their one desperate request and the answer they receive (77), and finally the reason they are doomed (78). Ibn Kathir marks that last movement explicitly, and it is what holds the passage together — it does not merely describe a punishment, it explains it. By the end of ayah 78 the reader knows why these people are where they are.

## Where the passage sits

Ibn Kathir notes the placement simply: "The description of the state of the blessed is followed by a description of the state of the doomed." The surah has just been speaking of those mindful of Allah, whose friendships alone survive the Day of Judgement — "Friends, on that day, will become enemies to one another, except those mindful of Allah" (43:67). Now the description turns to the other party.

## Ayat 74–75: a sentence with no gaps in it

**"Indeed, the wicked will be in the torment of Hell forever."** The word rendered "the wicked" is *al-mujrimūn*, which Ibn Kathir's text renders as "the criminals." And *khālidūn* — abiding, remaining — is the word that fixes the duration: to abide therein forever.

Then ayah 75 closes the two doors a suffering person normally reaches for.

**The first door is relief.** *Lā yufattaru ʿanhum* — "it will never be lightened for them." Ibn Kathir glosses this with four words that are the whole point: **"not even for one moment."** Every pain we know in this life has some texture to it — it rises and it ebbs, sleep interrupts it, medicine dulls it. What is described here has no such gap in it anywhere.

**The second door is hope.** *Wa hum fīhi mublisūn* — a word so dense that Ibn Kathir's translated text needs a whole phrase for it: "they will be plunged into destruction with deep regrets, sorrows and in despair therein." He then explains it in five words: **"they will despair of any goodness."** Sit with that second phrase alongside the first. It is not only pain; it is pain accompanied by the settled expectation that nothing good is coming.

## Ayah 76: no injustice was done

**"We did not wrong them, but it was they who were the wrongdoers."** Having described something so severe, the Qur'an immediately answers the objection the human heart raises. Ibn Kathir explains what makes the sentence just: they committed their wrong actions **"after proof had been established against them and Messengers had been sent to them, but they rejected them and rebelled, so they are to be punished accordingly."** He then seals the point with the Qur'an's own words: **"And your Lord is not at all unjust to (His) servants."**

Two things are packed into that gloss. First, nobody is punished for what they had no way of knowing — messengers came, the proof was established, the case was made. Second, the punishment is a response, not an initiative: it answers something they did, and it answers it in measure — "so they are to be punished accordingly." The wrong they suffer is their own wrong, returned to them.

This is a foundation of belief: Allah is perfectly just, and no one in the Fire will be able to say that no case was ever put to them.

## Ayah 77: the cry to Mālik

**"They will cry, 'O Mālik! Let your Lord finish us off.'"** Mālik, Ibn Kathir tells us, is **the keeper of Hell**.

And what is it they want from him? Not release, not forgiveness, not even relief — an end. Ibn Kathir spells out the request: **"let Him destroy our souls and give us some respite from our predicament."** Death has become the most they dare ask for. That single request tells you more about the Fire than a description of it could.

**Two ayat Ibn Kathir cites to show the request is impossible.** He brings *Fāṭir* 35:36 — "Neither will it have a complete killing effect on them so that they die nor shall its torment be lightened for them" — and *al-Aʿlā* 87:11–13, "But it will be avoided by the wretched, who will enter the great Fire. There he will neither die (to be in rest) nor live (a good living)." Neither dying nor living: held back from both of the exits by which relief usually comes.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir reports: Al-Bukhari said, "Hajjaj bin Minhal told us, Sufyan bin 'Uyaynah told us, from 'Amr bin 'Ata, from Safwan bin Ya'la that his father, may Allah be pleased with him, said, 'I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reciting on the Minbar'" — and then this very ayah, *"And they will cry: 'O Mālik! Let your Lord make an end of us.'"* A small, vivid detail, and worth sitting with: a Companion heard these words recited by the Prophet ﷺ from the pulpit.

**The answer.** *Qāla innakum mākithūn* — "He will say: Verily, you shall abide forever." That is the whole of the reply. No argument, no consolation, no explanation. Ibn Kathir's gloss: **"you will have no way out from it and no refuge."** Their request takes a full sentence; the reply is three words, and the ayah records nothing further from him.

## Ayah 78: the reason, finally stated

Ibn Kathir marks the turn precisely: "Then the reason why they are doomed will be given, which is their stubborn resistance to the truth."

**"We certainly brought the truth to you."** Ibn Kathir: **"We have explained it to you clearly and in detail."** Not hinted at, not left for the clever to decode — brought, and made plain. The failure was never a failure of information.

**"But most of you were hateful of the truth."** This is the diagnosis, and it is not what a modern reader expects. The problem was not that they found the message unconvincing; it is that they found it *unwelcome*. Ibn Kathir unpacks the state of such a soul as a chain of attitudes: **"your nature could not accept it and did not seek it; on the contrary, you followed and venerated falsehood, and you stood in the way of truth and refused it, and despised its followers."**

Read that slowly, because it is a portrait of a heart, not of an argument:

- **it did not seek** the truth — no appetite for it in the first place;
- **it followed and venerated falsehood** — the loyalties had already been given elsewhere;
- **it stood in the way of the truth and refused it** — active resistance, not passive doubt;
- **it despised the followers of the truth** — contempt for the people who carried it.

Note also the wording: "most of you." The ayah does not say all.

Ibn Kathir closes with the outcome of this self-knowledge: **"So they will blame themselves and will feel regret at the time when regret will not be of any benefit to them."** In ayah 75 they had already despaired of any good; now they blame themselves. This is the meaning of ayah 76 experienced from the inside — the wrongdoers themselves become the witnesses that no injustice was done.

## Living it

**Test yourself for appetite, not only for belief.** The people of ayah 78 had the truth explained to them clearly and in detail. What Ibn Kathir says they lacked was any seeking of it — their nature "did not seek it." So the useful question is not only "do I accept this?" but "do I want it?" — do I look forward to the Qur'an, or do I find reasons to postpone it?

**Notice what you venerate.** Ibn Kathir's sequence includes a heart already committed elsewhere — *you followed and venerated falsehood*. Whatever a person has made great in his own eyes will shape what he is willing to receive.

**Watch how you regard practising people.** In that same list, despising the followers of the truth sits alongside standing in its way and refusing it. Contempt for people because they take the religion seriously appears here as part of one pattern with rejecting the truth itself.

**Take the certainty of ayah 76 seriously — in both directions.** "And your Lord is not at all unjust to (His) servants." That is a comfort where you have been wronged in this world, and a warning where you are the one deciding. Allah's justice is not a slogan in this passage; it is the reason the punishment can be described so severely with no apology offered for it.

**Let ayah 75 shape your duʿāʾ.** The Fire is described here by the absence of two mercies — no lightening, not even for one moment, and no expectation of any goodness. Everything you presently have of ease, of rest between hardships, of a reason to expect good tomorrow, is a mercy you did not manufacture. The right response to this passage is not to dwell on the horror but to run to the One who is keeping it away from you — while the truth is still being brought to you clearly.

passages.title: Scheming answered, and no offspring for the Most Compassionate
passages.tafsir:
In Ibn Kathir's arrangement, these ayat follow directly on the description of the doomed and the reason given for their ruin — what he calls "their stubborn resistance to the truth." Allah had said, *"Indeed We have brought the truth to you"* (ayah 78), which Ibn Kathir explains as *"We have explained it to you clearly and in detail,"* and yet *"most of you have a hatred for the truth."*

What follows in our passage is what such people *do* with that hatred: they scheme (79), they whisper (80), and they say of the Most Compassionate that He has offspring (81). Each move is answered in turn: their scheme is met by His planning, their whispering is heard and written down, their claim is met by a courteous but devastating argument (81), then by pure glorification (82), and finally by an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ to leave them until the appointed Day (83).

That is the pattern to hold on to: **three human moves, and Allah's answer to each.**

## Ayah 79 — a plot answered by a plan

**"Or have they mastered some plan? Then We too are surely planning."**

Ibn Kathir reports Mujahid's brief and exact gloss: *"They wanted to plot some evil, but We are also planning."* He then places the ayah alongside a verse of Surat an-Naml: *"So they plotted a plot, and We planned a plan, while they perceived not"* (27:50).

What the ayah means is stated plainly by Ibn Kathir:

> "The idolators were trying their utmost to find ways of refuting the truth with falsehood, but Allah planned it so that the consequences of that would backfire on them."

That is the whole substance of the ayah. The plotting was real and it was strenuous — Ibn Kathir's phrase is that they were "trying their utmost." What they did not know was that the consequences would come back on the plotters themselves. Their design became the instrument of their own undoing.

There is a comfort buried here for anyone who has ever felt small before organised opposition. The ayah does not promise that the plotting will not happen. It promises that it will be answered — and answered by the One whose planning encloses theirs.

## Ayah 80 — the secret that was never secret

**"Or do they think that We do not hear their secrets and their private counsel? Yes indeed — and Our messengers are with them, recording."**

Plotting depends on privacy. So the very next ayah dismantles the privacy. Ibn Kathir glosses the pair of words *sirrahum wa najwāhum* — their secret and their private counsel — as **"what they say secretly and openly."** Between them, the two words close every gap: what is kept hidden and what is said out in the open. Nothing falls outside.

Then comes the reply, which Ibn Kathir renders as *"Yes (We do)."* Their assumption was that Allah does not hear. The reply overturns the assumption before it adds anything to it.

And what it adds is a second layer of witness. Ibn Kathir: *"'We know what they are doing, and the angels are also recording their deeds, major and minor.'"* Allah's own knowledge of what they are doing would have been sufficient. But alongside it there is a written record, kept by "Our messengers" — whom Ibn Kathir identifies as the angels — and it omits nothing, neither the grave nor the trivial.

So the two ayat work as a single blow. Ayah 79 says: *your plan will be answered.* Ayah 80 says: *and it was never hidden to begin with.*

## Ayah 81 — the "if" that is not a concession

**"Say: If the Most Compassionate had offspring, then I would be the first of the worshippers."**

This is the most easily misread ayah of the passage, so both of our commentators stop to guard it.

**Ibn Kathir** explains the sense as: *"if this were so, then I would worship Him on that basis, because I am one of His servants; I obey all that He commands me and I am not too arrogant or proud to worship Him."* And then, immediately, the safeguard: *"This conditional phrase does not mean that what is described could happen nor that is possible."* He cites in support: *"Had Allah willed to take a son, He could have chosen whom He willed out of those whom He created. But glory be to Him! He is Allah, the One, the Irresistible"* (39:4).

So the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to make his servanthood the point: whatever Allah commands, His servant obeys, without pride. Ibn Kathir's phrasing is worth sitting with — *I am not too arrogant or proud to worship Him.* The Messenger ﷺ is told to declare exactly that disposition of himself.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** draws out the argumentative etiquette in the ayah, and this is its most valuable contribution to the passage:

> "It does not mean that — Allah forbid — there is any possibility of Rahman (Allah) having offspring. What is really being said is that the Holy Prophet ﷺ is not denying your beliefs due to enmity or obstinacy, but because they are illogical. If precise logical arguments could prove the existence of offspring of Allah, he would certainly have accepted it. But every intellectual argument contradicts this possibility, and therefore there is no question of accepting it."

In other words: *I am not against you. I am against a claim that cannot be established.* And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then turns that into a general principle of how a Muslim argues:

> "This tells us that it is lawful, rather desirable, to declare during a debate with erring people that if their claim had been proved by strong arguments, it would have been accepted, because such a manner of speech may sometimes soften the heart of the opponent and may persuade him to accept the truth."

That is a striking permission. In a dispute over the greatest matter there is, the Messenger ﷺ is taught to open with a sentence that lowers the temperature and leaves the other man a way to walk towards the truth without humiliation. Not one letter of the creed is surrendered — the very next ayah is a thunderclap of glorification. But the manner is gentle, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells us why: because a softened heart may yet accept the truth.

## Ayah 82 — the glorification that answers everything

**"Glorified is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the Lord of the Throne, above what they ascribe."**

Having reasoned with them, the passage now simply declares. Ibn Kathir:

> "meaning, exalted and sanctified and glorified be the Creator of all things far above having any offspring, for He is Unique, One and Eternally Self-Sufficient. There is none equal to Him or like Him, and He does not have any offspring."

Every word of that gloss is load-bearing. He is **the Creator of all things** — and the claim of offspring would place something alongside Him rather than under Him. He is **Unique, One and Eternally Self-Sufficient** — and self-sufficiency needs nothing, least of all a child. **There is none equal to Him or like Him** — which closes the door on comparison altogether. And so the false description is not merely mistaken; the ayah declares Him exalted *above* it.

This is the shape of the whole passage in miniature. First the reasoned answer (ayah 81), then the pure affirmation (ayah 82). Argument has its place, but the believer's final ground is not that he has out-argued anyone; it is that he knows his Lord.

## Ayah 83 — leave them to their game

**"So let them indulge in falsehood and amuse themselves until they meet their Day which they have been promised."**

Ibn Kathir takes the three parts in order:

- **"So leave them to speak nonsense"** — *"means, in their ignorance and misguidance."*
- **"and play"** — *"in their world."*
- **"until they meet the Day of theirs which they have been promised"** — *"which is the Day of Resurrection, i.e., then they will come to know what their end and destination will be on that Day."*

Two things are worth noticing about this instruction.

First, it is not despair, and it is certainly not approval of what they are doing — Ibn Kathir has just called it ignorance and misguidance. It is a dismissal with a deadline. The word "until" is the whole point: their indulgence has a terminus already fixed and already promised. And Ibn Kathir's two-word gloss on "and play" — *in their world* — quietly measures the scope of the amusement. This world is the entire playing field. Beyond it, as he says, they will come to know what their end and destination will be.

Second, the Prophet ﷺ is told to step back. The truth had already been brought and, in Ibn Kathir's words on ayah 78, *"explained to you clearly and in detail"* — and the response was hatred of it, because, again in his words, *"you followed and venerated falsehood, and you stood in the way of truth and refused it, and despised its followers."* When a person has settled into that, more argument is not the remedy. So the Messenger ﷺ is told to leave them, and let the promised Day do what words could not.

## Living it

**Fear the recording more than the audience.** Ayah 80 is the most personally searching verse in the passage. What we say when no one is listening — the private message, the whispered arrangement — is heard, and it is written, "major and minor." A believer who takes that seriously acquires a kind of integrity that is the same in company and in solitude.

**Argue like ayah 81.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has handed us a method: say plainly that a proven claim would be accepted, show that no argument establishes this one, and keep the other person's heart in view throughout — because that manner "may sometimes soften the heart of the opponent." Firmness on the content, softness in the manner. That combination is far harder — and far more persuasive — than either alone.

**Know when to stop.** Ayah 83 teaches that there is a point at which continuing to argue is no longer the remedy. Deliver the truth clearly, as it was delivered "clearly and in detail," then leave the outcome to the Day that has already been promised.

**And when the scheming is against you**, hold ayah 79 in your heart. They plan; Allah plans. Nothing they whisper is unheard, and Ibn Kathir's assurance stands over all of it: Allah planned it so that the consequences would backfire on them.

passages.title: Allah in heaven and earth, and the Prophet's complaint
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat close Sūrah az-Zukhruf. Having rejected the claim that Allah has offspring, the passage now states positively who Allah is — the One worshipped by those in the heavens and those on the earth, the Sovereign of the heavens, the earth and all that is between them, the only One with whom is the knowledge of the Hour — then exposes the incoherence of people who admit He created them yet worship others alongside Him, and finally turns to the Prophet ﷺ himself: his complaint to his Lord about his people is recorded in the Qur'an, and his instruction is to turn away from them and say peace.

What holds the unit together is the movement from the highest truth about Allah down to the most human moment in the sūrah. It begins in the heavens and ends with a grieving heart and a quiet parting.

## Where the passage picks up

Just before our range, the Prophet ﷺ is told to say that if the Most Gracious had a son, he would be the first of the worshippers (ayah 81). Ibn Kathir explains the sense: *if this were so, then I would worship Him on that basis, because I am one of His servants; I obey all that He commands me and I am not too arrogant or proud to worship Him.* He adds that this conditional phrase does not mean that what is described could happen, nor that it is possible, comparing it with Allah's words, "Had Allah willed to take a son, He could have chosen whom He willed out of those whom He created. But glory be to Him! He is Allah, the One, the Irresistible" (39:4).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the argument is framed this way. The Prophet ﷺ is not denying their beliefs out of enmity or obstinacy, but because they are illogical; if precise logical arguments could prove it, he would certainly have accepted it — but every intellectual argument contradicts the possibility. From this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān derives a principle of debate: it is lawful, rather desirable, to declare during a debate with erring people that if their claim had been proved by strong arguments it would have been accepted, because such a manner of speech may sometimes soften the heart of the opponent and persuade him to accept the truth.

Ibn Kathir's comment on ayah 82 keeps the same theme in view: exalted and sanctified and glorified be the Creator of all things far above having any offspring, *for He is Unique, One and Eternally Self-Sufficient. There is none equal to Him or like Him, and He does not have any offspring.*

Then in ayah 83 the Prophet ﷺ is told to leave them — Ibn Kathir: to leave them *in their ignorance and misguidance*, playing *in their world*, until they meet the Day of Resurrection, when they will come to know what their end and destination will be on that Day.

## Ayah 84: worshipped in the heaven and on the earth

**وَهُوَ ٱلَّذِي فِي ٱلسَّمَآءِ إِلَٰهٞ وَفِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ إِلَٰهٞ** — *It is He Who is the only Deity in the heaven and the only Deity on the earth.*

This is not a statement about Allah occupying two places. Ibn Kathir gives the meaning plainly: **He is the Deity of those who are in the heavens and the Deity of those who are on earth; all of them worship Him and are humbled before Him.** The two spheres named in the ayah are two populations — those above and those below — and both have exactly one rightful object of worship, and He is one and the same. That is the whole point of the ayah as Ibn Kathir reads it: worship and humility, everywhere, directed to Him alone.

Ibn Kathir strengthens this by pairing the ayah with another: "And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth; He knows what you conceal and what you reveal, and He knows what you earn" (6:3), which he explains as meaning **He is the One who is called Allah in the heavens and on the earth**. That is, His name and His worship reach across the whole of creation; there is no upper realm with one deity and a lower realm with others.

Notice also what the ayah he cites places right beside that truth: knowledge of what you conceal and what you reveal, and of what you earn. And notice how our own ayah closes — **وَهُوَ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ**, *the All-Wise, the All-Knower.* The One worshipped above and below is the same One from whom nothing is hidden.

## Ayah 85: Blessed is the Owner of it all

**وَتَبَارَكَ ٱلَّذِي لَهُۥ مُلۡكُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَمَا بَيۡنَهُمَا** — *And Blessed be He to Whom belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, and all that is between them.*

Ibn Kathir unpacks the sovereignty first: **He is their Creator and Sovereign, the One Who is controlling them with none to resist or oppose His rule.** Then he ties the "blessedness" straight back to the argument of the sūrah: **Blessed and exalted be He far above the notion of His having a child. He is eternally free of all faults and shortcomings, because He is the Lord, the Exalted, the Almighty, the Sovereign of all things, Who is in control of all affairs.**

That is the logic in miniature, and it is worth reading slowly. The reason offered for His being far above having a child is not merely that the claim is offensive; it is *who He is* — the Sovereign of all things, in control of all affairs, eternally free of every fault and shortcoming. Ascribing offspring to such a One contradicts what He has just been described as.

Two clauses then follow that quietly reframe the reader's whole situation:

**وَعِندَهُۥ عِلۡمُ ٱلسَّاعَةِ** — *and with Whom is the knowledge of the Hour.* Ibn Kathir: **no one knows when it will happen except Him.**

**وَإِلَيۡهِ تُرۡجَعُونَ** — *and to Whom you will be returned.* Ibn Kathir: **each person will be requited for his deeds; if they are good, then he will be rewarded, and if they are bad, then he will be punished.** The address switches to "you" — the argument stops being about *them* and lands on whoever is listening.

## Ayah 86: the intercession the idols do not have

**وَلَا يَمۡلِكُ ٱلَّذِينَ يَدۡعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ ٱلشَّفَٰعَةَ** — *And those whom they invoke instead of Him have no power of intercession.*

Ibn Kathir identifies "those whom they invoke" as **the idols and false gods**, and the meaning of the clause as: **they are not able to intercede for them.** The objects of their worship simply cannot do this thing for them.

Then comes the exception: **إِلَّا مَن شَهِدَ بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَهُمۡ يَعۡلَمُونَ** — *except for those who bear witness to the truth knowingly, and they know.* Ibn Kathir explains: **the one who bears witness to the truth has knowledge and insight, so his intercession with Allah will avail, by His leave.**

Read the two halves together and the doctrine is clear. Intercession is real — but as Ibn Kathir words it, it belongs to the one who bears witness to the truth with knowledge and insight, and even then it avails *by Allah's leave*. It is not something the idols possess and not something they can extend to anyone. Whoever hopes for intercession must first be on the side of that testimony.

## Ayah 87: they know the answer and still turn away

**وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُمۡ مَّنۡ خَلَقَهُمۡ لَيَقُولُنَّ ٱللَّهُ** — *And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say: "Allah."*

Ibn Kathir: ask these idolaters who associate others in worship with Allah who created them, and **they will admit that He Alone is the Creator of all things and He has no partner in that. Yet despite that they still worship others alongside Him who have nothing and are able to do nothing.** His verdict on this is blunt: **This is the utmost foolishness and stupidity.**

That is the shape of the argument. It is not that they lack the information; by Ibn Kathir's account they will readily give the right answer. It is that the answer they give and the worship they practise have come apart. Hence the closing question, **فَأَنَّىٰ يُؤۡفَكُونَ** — *how then are they turned away?*

This is worth sitting with, because the pattern is not confined to Makkah. A person can hold a belief sincerely at the level of statement and live in another direction entirely. The Qur'an puts that as a question — *how then are they turned away?* — and treats it as astonishing rather than normal.

## Ayah 88: the Prophet's complaint

**وَقِيلِهِۦ يَٰرَبِّ إِنَّ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ قَوۡمٞ لَّا يُؤۡمِنُونَ** — *And his saying: "O my Lord! Verily, these are a people who believe not!"*

Ibn Kathir: **Muhammad ﷺ said this; he complained to his Lord about his people who did not believe in him, and said, 'O Lord, these people do not believe.'** He compares it with the ayah, "And the Messenger will say: 'O my Lord! Verily, my people deserted this Qur'an'" (25:30).

This reading is not one man's opinion. Ibn Kathir reports it as the view of **Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, Mujahid and Qatadah**, and notes that **Ibn Jarir** interpreted it this way. He then relates that **Al-Bukhari said** that ʿAbdullah — meaning Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him — recited this ayah with the wording *"And the Messenger will say: O my Lord!"* Mujahid's comment on the ayah is: **"Allah is stating what Muhammad said."** Qatadah's is: **"These are the words of your Prophet ﷺ, when he complained about his people to his Lord."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the ayah has been construed in different ways, and that its own rendering — *"And [Allah has the knowledge] of His prophet's saying, 'O my Lord, these are a people who do not believe'"* — is based on the construction adopted by Maulana Ashraf ʿAli Thanawi, with various other constructions given in Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī. So the scholars differ on exactly how the words attach to what precedes; but the content of the sentence — the Prophet's ﷺ complaint, raised to his Lord — is what both sources dwell on.

**Why this sentence sits here.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason with real force. The point of the sentence, it says, is that there are very serious reasons for Allah's wrath descending upon these disbelievers. On one side stand their severe crimes themselves. On the other stands this: the Messenger ﷺ, who was sent as a "blessing for the world" and an "interceder for the sinners", himself complains against them and says that these people do not believe, despite repeated good counsels given to them. That indicates, in its words, that they must have agonised the Prophet ﷺ to an extreme extent — otherwise "the blessing for the worlds" would not have made such a plaint merely on an ordinary hurt.

There is something tender in the shape of the words as Ibn Kathir describes them. The complaint is made *to* his Lord, about the people. And it stands in the Book of Allah, so that the grief of His Messenger ﷺ is on record. A believer worn down by people he cannot reach has been shown exactly where to take it.

## Ayah 89: turn aside, and say peace

**فَٱصۡفَحۡ عَنۡهُمۡ وَقُلۡ سَلَٰمٞۚ فَسَوۡفَ يَعۡلَمُونَ** — *So turn away from them, and say: Salam (peace!) But they will come to know.*

**فَٱصۡفَحۡ عَنۡهُمۡ** — Ibn Kathir: turn away **from the idolators**.

On **wa qul salām**, the two sources give complementary shades:

- **Ibn Kathir** reads it as forbearance in dealing: **do not respond to them in the same evil manner in which they address you; but try to soften their hearts and forgive them in word and deed.** Answer their ugliness with peaceable speech, still hoping for them.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** reads *salām* here as an idiomatic expression for the parting of ways — a "good-bye". It is careful to add that the instruction to say *salām* does not mean that *"Assalāmu ʿalaikum"* is to be said to them, since it holds that this salutation is not permissible for any non-Muslim; and it states (citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī) that the view of those who deduce from this ayah that saying *"Assalāmu ʿalaikum"* to non-Muslims is permissible **does not carry much weight**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then states the general counsel the ayah leaves for every preacher of truth — the same advice, it says, that is always given to every such preacher: one may reply to the arguments and doubts of opponents, but when they start talking ignorantly, foolishly, or are involved in hurling abuses, then instead of replying in their language, one should keep quiet.

**فَسَوۡفَ يَعۡلَمُونَ** — *but they will come to know.* Ibn Kathir calls this **a warning from Allah for them**, and then tells what followed: **His punishment, which cannot be warded off, struck them, and His religion and His word was supreme. Subsequently Jihad and striving were prescribed until the people entered the religion of Allah in crowds, and Islam spread throughout the east and the west.** The one told to fall silent was not told to give up. He was told that the outcome is not in his hands and not in theirs.

With that, Ibn Kathir closes: **And Allah knows best. This is the end of the Tafsir of Surat Az-Zukhruf.**

## Living it

- **Argue for the truth, but argue honestly.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point on ayah 81 is a discipline: be the kind of person who would accept a claim if strong arguments proved it, and say so in a debate. It may soften the heart of the one you are speaking to.
- **Watch the gap in ayah 87.** By Ibn Kathir's account the idolaters would readily admit that Allah alone created them, and still worshipped what has nothing and can do nothing. The question to ask of oneself is not "do I believe Allah made me?" but "does anything in how I live contradict the answer I would give?"
- **Do not look for intercessors beside Allah.** Ayah 86 removes the premise: the idols and false gods are not able to intercede. Where intercession does avail, it is for the one who bears witness to the truth with knowledge and insight — and it avails by Allah's leave.
- **Take the complaint to Allah.** Ayah 88 shows the Prophet ﷺ complaining to his Lord about people who would not believe — and Allah recording it in the Qur'an. Grief over people who will not listen is not weakness of faith; the place for it is before Allah.
- **Know when to stop talking.** Ayah 89 asks for two things at once: not answering evil with evil, but trying to soften hearts and forgiving in word and deed (Ibn Kathir); and falling silent rather than replying in kind when speech turns to foolishness and abuse (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). The last words of the sūrah — *they will come to know* — are the reason you can afford to leave quietly.
